en: Śaṃkara: Salutation to that All-Knowing One, who is consciousness, all-pervading, everything, dwelling in the cave of the heart of all beings, and who transcends all objects. (Upadeśasāhasrī I.1.1)
Having completed all the rites beginning with marriage and the establishment of the sacred fires, the Veda now proceeds to expound the knowledge of Brahman. (Samhitopaniṣad I.2)
Karmas exist for the sake of conjunction with a body; when there is conjunction with a body, the pleasant and the unpleasant are inevitable.
From these arise attachment and aversion, and from those, further actions.
From that, merit and demerit arise for the ignorant one, and from those, again, the conjunction with a body;
thus this cycle of existence proceeds eternally, like a wheel, with great force.
Ignorance is its root; therefore, its abandonment is desired.
It begins with the knowledge of Brahman; from that, the supreme good arises. (Samupad I.1.5)
Knowledge alone, not action, leads to the destruction of ignorance because it is not opposed to it;
for as long as ignorance is not abandoned, there can be no destruction of passion and hatred. (Samyukta-upaniṣad 1.6)
In the absence of the destruction of passion and hatred, action certainly arises from defects;
therefore, for the sake of the supreme good, knowledge alone is prescribed here.
Indeed, as long as one lives, action must be performed in that manner;
for it serves as an auxiliary to knowledge with respect to liberation. (Samupad I.1.8)

Just as knowledge, so too must action be performed by those seeking liberation, because there is no difference in their being enjoined [by scripture], and because of the traditional teaching regarding the sin [incurred by its omission]. (Samupad I.1.9)
Surely knowledge, having its fruit as certain, does not depend on anything else, just as the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, though its result is certain, nevertheless depends on other factors. (Samupad I.1.10)
"Likewise, knowledge that has a certain fruit always requires ritual action;
thus some maintain this, not because of any opposition toward ritual action. (Samupad I.1.11)
For action performed with egoism would indeed be contrary to knowledge;
and that which is the cognition of the self as changeless is proclaimed here as knowledge. (Samayupad I.1.12)
"The thought 'I am the agent' and 'this shall be mine'—thus does karma proceed. Knowledge would be dependent upon the object; ritual injunction would be dependent upon the agent. (Samupad I.1.13)
It destroys the causal factors, just as knowledge destroys the notion [of water] in saline soil;
having taken hold of the conviction that "this is the truth," it resolves to perform action. (Samupad I.1.14)
Therefore, because they are mutually contradictory, action cannot be performed together with knowledge by one who knows this; for that reason, action must be abandoned by the seeker of liberation.

The innate perception of embodied beings as being non-different from their bodies and so forth arises from ignorance; as long as that persists, the injunctions regarding karma remain in force for living beings. (Samupad I.1.16)
By means of the teaching "not this, not this," the body and other such things are excluded, leaving only the Self;
for the sake of realizing the undifferentiated Self, ignorance is thereby dispelled. (Samupad I.1.17)
How could that [ignorance], once ceased, be produced again according to valid means of knowledge?
For it is only when the pure inner self (pratyagātman) is devoid of any distinction [from ignorance] that [such production would occur]. 1.18.
If one is not born again, how could there be the notion that "I am the doer" or "I am the enjoyer"?
Therefore, the realization "I am Being" (sat) is accompanied by knowledge (vidyā). 1.19.
Because it was said, "He excelled," the renunciation (nyāsa) is thus established by the Śruti;
for it is said that among the Vājasaneyins, this [renunciation] is superior to all ritual acts ending with those of the mind.
"Since immortality is heard [to result from knowledge], therefore action must be abandoned by those seeking liberation;
as for the statement that it is like the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, to this the following is said: (Samupad I.1.21)
Because action is accomplished by multiple factors and because its fruits are distinct, knowledge is the opposite of that; therefore, the illustrative example would be dissimilar.

Since it has a fruit as its purpose, like agriculture and other such acts, knowledge requires the supplementation of other rituals; but what else could the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice require? (Samupad I.1.23)
But transgression belongs only to him in whom egoism is found;
when there is a desire for the fruits of egoism, they do not exist for one who knows the Self.
Therefore, for the sake of destroying ignorance, for the cessation of saṃsāra, and for the instruction of the knowledge of Brahman, this Upaniṣad has been commenced. (SamUpad I.1.25)
From the root *sad* preceded by *upa-ni*, with the suffix *kvip*, the word *upaniṣad* is formed;
it is so called because of the state of making [the self] mild and likewise because of the destruction of the embryo and so forth. (SamUpad I.1.26)
Thus ends the section on consciousness. Samyuktopaniṣad I, 1.
Because it is impossible to negate [it], that which remains as "not this, not this" is understood with certainty as: "This is not I; this is not I. (Samyukta Upanishad I.2.1)
This [world] is perceived as "this" or "that," arising from the self and falling within the scope of speech-based activity;
because its origin from the self has been negated, it cannot again attain the status of a valid means of knowledge. (Samupad I.2.2)
A subsequent cognition does not arise without subverting the preceding cognition;
the Seer is one and self-established, and because it is the fruit [of all], it is not subverted. (SamUpad I.2.3)
Having transcended this forest corrupted by grief, delusion, and the like, one attains one's own self, just as the man from Gandhāra recovered himself from the forest. (Samyukta Āgama I, 2.4)
Thus ends the section on prohibitions. (Samyukta Āgama Upadeśa I, 2)
If the Lord were not the Self, one would not maintain "I am He";
if the Lord is the Self, the knowledge "I am He" is that which removes all else. (SamUpad I.3.1)

If qualities such as non-materiality and so forth are considered to belong to something other than the self, what would be gained for this [self] by them if it were unknowable? But if they belong to the self, there is the removal of the notion of "other. (Samupad I.3.2)
Therefore, for the purpose of negating false superimposition, let [the texts] such as "not gross" be accepted;
for if they serve to negate [superimposition] regarding another [object], that is indeed the description of emptiness.

If it were intended that [the Self] other than the inner self (pratyagātman) is what one desires to know, then the statement, "For He is without breath, without mind, pure," would be meaningless. (SamUpad I.3.4)
Thus ends the section on the Lord (Īśvara). Samyukta Āgama, Chapter 1, Section 3.
How can karma sprout when its seed—the notion of "I"—is scorched by the fire of the realization that there is no such "I"? (Samādhipādādhikāra 4.1)
If growth were to occur as seen [in the case of a visible seed], that [growth] would not be admitted to have another action [as its cause].
When that [visible cause] has ceased, how could that [growth] exist? We ask you: let it be explained. (Samupad I.4.2)

Due to the capacity for initiating the body and so forth, knowledge that has the Real as its object would produce its fruit by overcoming [the power of] karma; however, knowledge arises at the end of karma. (Samupad I.4.3)
For these two—experience and knowledge—are the fruits of action that has been undertaken;
their non-contradiction is logical, whereas for the other [action], there is a difference in nature.

Just as the knowledge that the body is the self is sublated by the knowledge that the self is not the body, so too does such knowledge arise regarding the Self alone; he in whom this occurs is liberated, even against his will. (Samyukta Upaniṣad 1.4.5)
[“Therefore, all this has been established; the application has been declared by us.
Thus ends the section on the notion of “I” (ahampratyaya), Samputa I.4.]
Just as the sage Udaṅka, fearing urine, did not accept the nectar, so too living beings,
out of fear that their karma will perish, do not grasp at the knowledge of the Self.
To one established in the Buddha-nature, the self appears as if moving and as if meditating;
just as trees appear to move to one traveling by boat, such is the delusion of saṃsāra.

Just as one standing on a boat perceives the movement of mountains in the opposite direction, so too is the transmigratory existence of the Self; for the Śruti says, "It is as if it were meditating. (Samyukta Upaniṣad I.5.3)
For consciousness arises pervaded by the reflection of pure awareness;
through this appearance of sound and other objects within the intellect, the world is deluded. (Samādhipādopadeśa 5.4)
The "I" consists in the manifestation of consciousness, and its being-for-that [the object] is its being directed toward that;
if the "this"-portion were removed, that supreme experience would not exist.
Thus ends the section on the suspicion of urine. // Samyukta Āgama I, 5 //
Just as the self is not distinguished by one's own hand when it has been cut off and discarded,
so too it is not distinguished by any remaining thing whatsoever by which it might be qualified.
Therefore, every qualification is equal to a hand that has been severed;
because they are non-self, the knower is thus liberated from all qualifications. 1.6.2
Just as all these ornaments are merely qualifications, so too is all this ignorance; therefore, when the Self is known, all that is unreal becomes non-existent.
The Self alone, as pure consciousness, should always be grasped while abandoning the object of knowledge;
for even that which is grasped as "I" is like a limb that has fallen away. (Samyutta-Upaniṣad 1.6.4)

Whatever portion of this [world] there may be that is other than itself is a qualification; where the removal of qualifications is established, it is the Knower, just as in the case of the "owner of brindled cows. (Samupad I.6.5)
In the realization "I am this [body]," the wise should abandon the notion that "the Self is not [the body]";
however, the remaining portion, "I am Brahman," may persist due to the persistence of past impressions. (Samupad I.6.6)
Thus ends the section on cutting. (Samyukta Āgama Upadhi-varga 1.6)
"Whatever is always perceived by me, wherever it may be, is mounted upon the intellect;
therefore, I am the Supreme Brahman, omniscient and omnipresent."
Just as one is the witness of the movements of one's own intellect, so too is one the witness regarding others;
therefore, another cannot be removed nor can he be added, for another is indeed myself.
The Self possesses neither mutability, impurity, nor materiality;
because it is the witness of all cognitions, its experience is not limited like that of the intellect.
Just as the red and other forms are manifested in a gem when it is in the sunlight, so too is everything perceived within me by means of me, as if by that very light. 7.4.
The visible object exists within the intellect; when the intellect is present, it exists, and in its absence, it does not.
Since the seer is always the seer, therefore duality does not exist. (Samyukta Upaniṣad I.7.5)
Just as the intellect perceives the non-existence of the Supreme due to lack of discrimination, so too,
through discrimination, it realizes that there is nothing other than the Supreme, and even itself does not exist.
Thus ends the chapter on that which is mounted upon the intellect. Samyuktopaniṣad I,7.
In my view, the nature of consciousness is self-evident; your association with flavors and the like is caused by delusion.
Therefore, no fruit can come to me from your activity, because of the abandonment of all distinctions.
Having abandoned here the state of being an effect composed of illusion, always come to peace from unreal striving;
for I am the supreme Brahman, eternally liberated, unborn, one, and devoid of duality.
And I am always equal toward all beings, being alone, all-pervading, imperishable, and auspicious like space;
I am continuous, partless, and actionless, supreme. Therefore, there is no fruit for me here from your efforts.
"I am one, and nothing other than that is desired; likewise, I do not belong to anyone, being unattached.
Since I am of the nature of non-attachment, I have no need for what is done by you, because of our non-duality."

Reflecting that people are deeply attached to both the fruit and the cause, I have therefore composed this discourse for the sake of liberating them, as a means to awaken them to the true meaning of the nature of reality. (Samādhirāja Sūtra Upadeśa 1.8.5)
If a person reflects upon this dialogue, they are liberated from the onset of the great fear of ignorance;
and such a person, forever freed from desire, dwells without sorrow, equanimous, a knower of the Self, and happy. (Samyukta Āgama 8.6)
Thus ends the section on the nature of consciousness. // SamUpad I,8 //
Subtlety and pervasiveness are to be known as belonging to smell and the other elements in successive order,
ending with the inner self, through the progressive abandonment of each preceding one.
The internal earth is equal in extent to the external earth in its measure;
likewise, the other elements, beginning with water, are to be known in their entirety.
Just as space is all-pervading prior to the arising of air and the other elements,
so am I alone— eternally all, pure consciousness, all-pervading, and non-dual.
All living beings, from Brahmā down to the immovable, are known as my city;
from what else could defects such as desire, anger, and the like arise in me? (Samyukta Upaniṣad 1.9.4)
Just as a child perceives the blue sky as defiled, so do people perceive me—the Lord who dwells within all beings—as always touched by the defects of the elements. (Samyutta Nikāya Upadeśa 1.9.5)
Because the intellects of all living beings are always illuminated by my consciousness,
all creatures are eternally my own, for I am omniscient and free from all taint.
That which is born is to be known through knowledge as being like the cognition of a dream;
therefore, knowledge is eternally without an object, and thus duality does not exist. (Samupad I.9.7)
For the knower is said to be eternal, yet in deep sleep it is empty of anything else;
the waking knower, however, exists through ignorance, and that which is perceived therein should be understood as unreal. (Samyutta-Upaniṣad I.9.8)
Just as sight and the other [faculties] do not possess the status of being an object because they lack the quality of having form (*rūpavattva*) and so forth,
it is understood that in the same way, the Great One (*bhūman*) does not possess the status of being an object of consciousness.
Thus ends the section on subtlety. // Samyukta Āgama I, 9 //
The nature of pure vision is like the sky, supreme, once-and-for-all manifest, unborn, one, and imperishable;
that which is untainted, all-pervading, and non-dual—that alone am I, eternally liberated, Om. (SamUpad I, 10.1)

But the Seer is pure, my nature is changeless, and by its very essence I have no object whatsoever; unborn and established in the Self, I am the perfectly full plenitude everywhere—in front, behind, above, below, and all around. (Samyukta Upaniṣad 1.10.2)

I am unborn and indeed immortal, likewise ageless and deathless, self-luminous, all-pervading, and non-dual; I am neither cause nor effect, exceedingly pure, eternally satisfied, and therefore liberated—Om. (Samyukta Upaniṣad I, 10.3)
I have no perception whatsoever of deep sleep, waking, or dreaming, for here this delusion is like a dream.
Since they are non-existent both by themselves and from another's perspective, I am always the Fourth alone—the non-dual Seer.

The continuum of body, intellect, senses, and suffering is not mine, nor am I it, because I am changeless; and likewise, this continuum is non-existent because of the non-existence of a sentient being, for it is like what is seen by one who sleeps.
But this is the truth: I have no modification, for there is no cause for change in me because of my non-duality;
there is neither merit nor sin, neither liberation nor bondage, and there is no state of caste or stage of life arising from the body.
Being without beginning and devoid of qualities, I have neither action nor fruit; therefore, I am the supreme non-dual one.
Just as the all-pervading sky is not defiled, so indeed am I, though situated within the body, due to my subtlety.

And I am always equal toward all beings, the Lord, indeed supreme and most excellent beyond both the perishable and the imperishable; though I am the reality of the Supreme Self and likewise non-dual, I am nevertheless enveloped by ignorance through perversion.

The Self, isolated from ignorance, mental cultivation, and karmas, unobstructed and utterly stainless, enriched with the powers of vision and the rest, I abide as non-dual in my own nature, immovable like the sky. (SamUpad I.10.9)
"I am the Supreme Brahman"—this is the word of the Śruti for one whose self-vision is characterized by certainty: "He is not born again.
Nor indeed is a fruit produced when the seed is absent; therefore, there is no further birth, and thus freedom from delusion. (Samyutta Upadeśa I.10.10)

"This is mine," "it was such for you in the past," "I am thus," and "another is otherwise"—such is the delusion of these people, who constantly conceptualize within the ever-equal, non-dual, and auspicious Brahman. (Samyukta Upanishad I, 10.11)
In that non-dual knowledge which is exceedingly pure for the great-souled ones, there is neither sorrow nor delusion;
in the absence of those two, there is indeed neither karma nor birth—this is the firm conclusion of those who know the Veda. (Samyukta Upaniṣad I, 10.12)
He who, while awake, does not perceive duality as if in deep sleep, and who, even while perceiving duality, perceives it as non-dual;
likewise, he who, even while acting, is actionless—he alone is the knower of the Self, and no other. This is the certainty here. (Samyutta Upadeśa 1.10.13)
Thus has this supreme vision of the ultimate truth been declared by me, as determined in the Vedānta.
If one becomes certain of this, one is liberated; one is not smeared by actions, just like the sky. (Samnyāsa Upaniṣad 1.14)
Thus ends the section on "seeing. (Samyukta Āgama, Chapter 1, Section 10)
The state of being a witness is self-established for living beings, and their difference from that [witness] arises from ignorance;
therefore, this otherness is negated by the teaching "Thou art That."
The scripture, stating that immortality consists of this much alone and that nothing else is an auxiliary to knowledge, sublates action along with its marks. (Samyukta Upaniṣad I.11.2)
For me, who am changeless and observe the activity of all minds without distinction, how could there be any differentiation whatsoever?
The activity of the mind and the mind itself are seen by the waking observer to be like a dream;
because both are absent in the state of supreme serenity (saṃprasāda), [the Self] is pure consciousness alone, all-pervading, and non-dual.
Just as a dream is real until one awakens, so too is the identification of the body with the self;
likewise, the validity of perception and other means of knowledge exists in the waking state only until there is the realization of the Self. (Samyutta-upadeśa 1.11.5)
Abiding in all beings like space, free from the defects of beings, the witness, the conscious one, devoid of qualities, pure—“I am indeed Brahman alone. (Samnyāsa Upaniṣad I.11.6)
I am the Self, other than the activities of name and form, possessing an eternally liberated nature;
I am the Supreme Brahman, pure consciousness alone, ever non-dual.
Those who know "I am Brahman, and I am the doer and the enjoyer," are ruined by both knowledge and action; they are atheists, without a doubt. (Samyukta Upanishad I.11.8)
Just as the connection of the self with the fruits of dharma and adharma is accepted as unperceived,
so too should its state of being Brahman and its liberation through knowledge be accepted on the basis of scripture.
Those impressions, such as those of saffron dye and so forth, are indeed experienced here by those who see dreams; therefore, the one who is distinct from them is pure consciousness alone.
Just as a sword drawn from its scabbard is seen in a dream as devoid of cause and effect, so too is the self-luminous knower.

For the wise one who has awakened from being pressed, the natural state is expressed by the statement beginning with "not this," which serves to remove the imagined [superimposition]. (Samupad I, 11.12)

Just as the world, including great kings and others, is imagined by me, so too should one know that the duality—form along with its latent impressions—exists within a dream. (Samādhirāja Sūtra Upadeśa 11.13)
Action should be performed by means of the body, the *liṅga*, and the self, which consist of latent impressions (*vāsanā*);
however, because my true nature is "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), no action is to be performed by me anywhere. (Samupad I.11.14)
There is no hope for immortality from that [action], because action has ignorance as its cause;
since liberation has knowledge as its cause, it does not depend on anything other than that.
The Self—which is immortal, fearless, unafflicted, and beyond "not this"—is dear to me;
whatever is contrary to this, one should abandon it along with all activity. (Samyukta Upaniṣad I.11.16)
Thus ends the section on the nature of the seer. // SamUpad I,11 //
Just as one perceives a body situated in light as being illuminated, so the mind, appearing as the seer, conceives "I am the seer. (Samyukta Upaniṣad I.12.1)
Whatever is perceived in the world, with that the fool identifies the Self; therefore, he does not find the Self. (Samnyāsa Upaniṣad I.12.2)
Just as there is the realization of the tenth [person] as being of the nature of the nine, so too,
in relation to the objects of perception, this world is deluded in that very way and not otherwise.
Tell me, how could two contradictory cognitions—"You do it" and "You do that"—which are simultaneous and have a single locus, be logically possible? 1.12.4.
Suffering belongs to one who identifies with the body, not to one who is bodiless by nature;
for the sake of abandoning that [identification], "That thou art" is said to the Seer, as in the case of deep sleep.
When the shadow of the seer is mounted upon the vision, like the reflection of a face in a mirror, the yogi, perceiving that sign, thinks, "The Self has been seen. (Samyukta Upanishad I.12.6)
If he knows that other condition [of the mind] to be deluded and distinct from the Seer, he alone is the best among yogis; no other could be so, without a doubt. (Samādhipādopadeśa 1.12.7)
Since that which is the knower of consciousness is said to be "Thou," He must be its experience; therefore, any experience other than that is false.
Since the nature of seeing is always eternal in me, how could both seeing and non-seeing occur? Therefore, no experience other than that [Self] is admitted.
Just as the heat residing in the sun is the object of the eye when it falls upon the body,
so too, one who abides in *sattva* is likewise the object of the eye here in this world.
The "this" portion has been negated; the Knower is like space, of one uniform essence, non-dual, eternally liberated, and likewise pure. I am that Brahman, the absolute. (Samyukta Upanishad I.12.11)
For the knower, no other supreme knower exists apart from him;
therefore, I am the supreme liberated knower within all beings at all times.
He who knows the unimpaired vision of the Self, as well as its state of non-agency and its nature as Brahman, is one who has realized the Self; no other is so.

"I am indeed known, yet unknowable; pure and eternally liberated"—even such a discriminative notion of the intellect is not [the Self], because it is an object of perception and is subject to destruction. (SamUpad I.12.14)
However, the vision of the Self is unlost, since it is not something to be produced by causal agents;
rather, its state of being produced has been merely imagined through another, visible vision.
The agency of the self is false because it depends on the notion that the body is the self;
the realization "I do nothing at all" is true, as it arises from valid means of knowledge.
Agency depends upon causal factors, while non-agency is inherent by nature;
it is firmly established that the cognition of "I am the doer" and "I am the enjoyer" is indeed false. (Samādhipradīpa I.12.17)
Thus, when the true nature [of the self] has been understood through scripture and inference, how could this notion—"I am the one to be enjoined"—possibly be true? (Samupad I.12.18)
Just as space is the innermost of all, for I am indeed within even space—
changeless, immovable, pure, undecaying, liberated, and eternally non-dual.
Thus ends the section on the Manifested, Samyutta Nikāya Upadeśa I, 12.

Because I am without eyes, there is no seeing for me; likewise, what hearing can there be for one without ears? Because I am without speech, there can be no speaking; and because I am without mind, how could there be thought? (Samyukta Āgama I, 13.1)
For that which is without breath there is no action; in the absence of intellect there is no knower.
Therefore, knowledge and ignorance do not exist for me, who am the light of pure consciousness alone.
Of that which is eternally liberated, pure, immutable, unwavering, immortal,
imperishable, and likewise always bodiless.
Hunger or thirst, grief or delusion, old age or death—these do not exist for me, because I am bodiless and all-pervading like space. (Samyukta Āgama I, 13.4)
Because I am intangible, I have no touch; because I am not a tongue, I have no perception of taste.
For me, who am of the nature of eternal consciousness, there is never knowledge or ignorance.
But that mental modification which is visual and colored by form is indeed always seen by the eternal vision of the Self. (Samyukta Āgama I.13.6)
Likewise, those functions associated with the other sense organs that perceive objects,
as well as memory and the forms of passion and so forth, exist solely within the internal mind.
In the same way, the dream-activities of another are seen by the mind;
therefore, the vision of the Seer is eternal, pure, infinite, and absolute.
"Due to a lack of discrimination in this regard, that [Self] is perceived as impermanent and impure;
likewise, through the visible limiting adjuncts, it is perceived as happy or suffering, and as 'I'. (Samādhipāda 1.8)
"This world, by means of which it enters into saṃsāra, conceives that one who is deluded is indeed deluded, and likewise that one who is pure is indeed pure. (Samādhipradīpa I.13.10)

If one desires liberation, one should always remember the Self here as taught in the scriptures—devoid of sight and other faculties, both internal and external, unborn, and eternally free. (Samupad I, 13.11)
And because of scriptural statements such as "I am without eyes," etc., my senses do not always exist;
for there is the declaration in the Atharva Veda: "Indeed, I am without breath and without mind, pure. (Samkhyakārikābhāṣya I.13.12)
And the absence of sound and the other [sensory objects] is heard by me in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad:
"For I am indeed without breath, without mind, and eternally changeless. (Samnyāsa Upaniṣad 1.13.13)
Therefore, there is no distraction for me, and consequently, there is no meditative absorption for me;
for either distraction or absorption would belong only to a mind that is subject to change.
How could that duality belong to me, who am mindless and pure? For me, who am bodiless, pervasive, and unchanging due to the state of being without mind, how could such duality exist?
Thus, as long as there was ignorance, so long did activity belong to me—though I am eternally liberated, pure, and forever awakened. (Samupad I.13.16)

Whether it be meditative absorption or non-absorption, or whatever other task there may be—having meditated upon and realized Me, they consider themselves to have accomplished all that was to be done. (Samyukta-upaniṣad I.13.17)
I am Brahman; I am everything; I am pure, enlightened, and eternally free from darkness.
I am unborn, all-pervading, undecaying, immortal, and inexhaustible.
Other than Me, no other perceiver exists among all beings;
I am the supervisor of karma, the witness, the conscious one, eternal, devoid of qualities, and non-dual.
I am neither existent nor non-existent, nor both; I am solely the auspicious one.
For me, who am eternally the Seer, there is no twilight, no night, and no day.
Just as space is devoid of all forms, subtle, and non-dual, so too am I separated from even that; I am Brahman alone, thus non-dual.
"Just as there may be a distinction in space due to its various cavities, so too is this distinction of 'my self' and 'his self' imagined within the One. (Samyukta Upanishad I.13.22)

Difference and non-difference, as well as unity and multiplicity— how could these conceptualized distinctions exist within me, who am one, with respect to the known, the knower, the goal, and the goer?
For me there is nothing to be abandoned and nothing to be acquired, since I am changeless;
I am eternally liberated, likewise eternally pure, eternally awakened, devoid of qualities, and non-dual.
Thus, one who is composed should always know the Self as everything;
having known Me abiding within his own body, the seer becomes liberated and steadfast. (Samyukta Upaniṣad I.13.25)

When one thus knows the true meaning of reality, one is one who has accomplished what was to be done, a perfected one, a yogi, and indeed a brahmin; otherwise, one becomes a destroyer of the self. (Samyukta Upanishad I, 13.26)
This definitive meaning of the Vedas has indeed been declared by me in brief;
it should be taught to peaceful renunciants by one whose intellect is disciplined. (Samyukta Upanishad I.13.27)
Thus ends the section on the absence of eyesight. (Samyukta Āgama I, 13)
For in dreams and in memory, the appearance of forms such as jars is observed; therefore, it is inferred that previously, at that time, a cognition possessing that same form must have been perceived.
Just as the body seen in a dream while wandering for alms is not oneself, so too, that which is the seer is indeed other than the body perceived while awake. (Samyukta-upaniṣad 1.14.2)
Just as copper poured into a mold takes on the appearance of that mold, so too the mind, pervading forms and other objects, is certainly seen to take on their appearance. (Samādhipradīpa I.14.3)

Or, just as light, acting as a manifestor, may take on the form of that which is manifested, so too the cognition, because it manifests all objects, appears as having the form of those objects. (SamUpad I.14.4)
For it is cognition alone that has been seen by men as having the very form of the object even previously;
if it were not so, how could one see [it] in a dream? And from where would there be the form of the remembered [object]?
Its very nature as a manifestor is its being perceived through the forms of color and so forth;
and its state as a seer is likewise [the perception] of the visible object. For there would be a pervasion [of these] upon the arising of cognition.
Since all cognitions in all bodies are illumined by me through the light of pure consciousness alone, I am therefore the Self of all. (Samupad I, 14.7)
The instrument, the object, the agent, the action, and the fruit are all [mere] cognition in a dream;
since they are seen thus even in the waking state, the seer must therefore be otherwise.
The intellect and the rest are non-self by virtue of being of the nature of what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted;
the self, as the agent of abandonment and acceptance, is neither to be discarded nor grasped. (Samyutta-upadeśa I.14.9)

When [the Self] is pure within and without, a solid mass whose sole essence is consciousness, how can anything else—whether external or internal—be conceived as something to be abandoned? (Samyutta-upaniṣad I.14.10)
If that Self which remains after the negation of "not this, not this" is accepted as the Self by the knower of Brahman, how could he strive for anything beyond that? (Samyukta Upanishad I.14.11)
"I am indeed Brahman alone, eternally transcending hunger and other such needs;
how could I ever be one who possesses effects?"—one should thus reflect straightforwardly. (SamUpanishad I.14.12)

Just as one who has reached the far bank of a river, while standing there, desires to go even further, so too does the knower of the Self, while remaining here, desire to perform other actions. (Samnyāsa Upaniṣad 1.14.13)
If even one who knows the Self should possess the tendency toward rejection and acquisition, he should be known as unworthy of liberation; he has certainly vomited up the Brahman.

For the world, together with the sun, is indeed the vital breath; therefore, neither day nor night can exist for one who knows the vital breath, much less for the knower of Brahman in the non-dual state.
For the Self does not remember itself, nor could it forget itself, since its consciousness is undiminished;
even the notion that "the mind remembers" is a cognition born from ignorance. (Samyukta Upaniṣad I.14.16)
For the knower, the Self to be known is indeed other; it is traditionally held to be constructed by ignorance.
When that [construct] is removed by knowledge, like a snake from a rope, the non-dual [Self remains]. (SamUpad I.14.17)
Since there is an absence of agent, object, and fruit, [reality] is indeed unborn, both internally and externally.
Regarding that state where [one thinks] "mine" and "I," to whom could it belong, and from what could it arise? (Samyukta Āgama Upanishad I, 14.18)
For this notion that "this is the self" and "this is what belongs to the self" is constructed by ignorance;
since this [notion] does not exist when there is the oneness of the Self, how can there be a fruit when the seed is absent? (Samyukta Āgama Upadeśa I, 14.19)
That Imperishable is indeed the seer, the hearer, the thinker, and the knower;
it is not something other than the seer and so forth. Therefore, I am the seer, the Imperishable.
Since everything—both the stationary and the moving—is endowed with activities such as seeing and so forth, it is therefore entirely imperishable;
thus, I am the imperishable Self of all.
He who perceives himself as having no remaining duties, as one whose nature is actionless yet the fruit of his own actions,
and as being free from "mine-ness" and egoism— he truly sees.
If it is known that "mine," "I," "effort," and "desire" are by their very nature empty even with respect to a self, then remain established in well-being; what is the use of further endeavors?
He who perceives the self as the agent of "I-making" and likewise as the knower is indeed one who does not know the self;
he who knows otherwise is the knower of the self. (Samyukta Upaniṣad I.14.24)
Just as the identity of the self with the body and so forth is maintained despite their difference,
so too, due to a lack of discernment regarding the agent, the self is regarded as being identical with the action and its fruit.
Sight, hearing, thought, and cognition are always seen by people in dreams;
because these have the nature of the Self, the Self is therefore directly perceived.
For that knower of the Self who has no fear of the next world nor fear of death, even the lords including Brahmā and Indra are objects of pity.
What is the use for him of lordship over the gods or even of the status of Brahmā,
if his thirst— which arises from all forms of wretchedness and is inherently unwholesome— has been severed in every respect?
When one's cognition of "I" as the self and the cognition of "mine" as belonging to the self are both devoid of an objective referent,
then that person becomes a knower of the self.
Whether the adjuncts such as the intellect exist or do not exist, there is no difference [in the Self];
for that Self which is the knower, how could it have any effect? (Samupad I.14.30)

When the sky is serene, stainless, and non-dual, consisting of the single essence of pure wisdom, tell me: for those in whom the realization of the Self has arisen, what other task remains to be desired?
He who, seeing himself as dwelling within all beings and his enemy as dwelling within himself, still desires [to harm the other], surely wishes to cool the fire. (Samudrapada I, 14.32)
The Self, which follows the vital breaths of wisdom, moves within the range of the senses and so forth like a shadow;
for it is said, "It meditates, as it were," because it is indeed pure and liberated by its own nature.
For me, who am without breath, without mind, likewise without association, all-pervading like space, and pure consciousness—how could there be any effect? (Samyukta Upanishad I.14.34)
I do not perceive non-concentration in me, who am forever changeless, pure, and stainless Brahman; nor is there anything else for me to purify.
And likewise, I must go; yet for Him who is all-pervading and immovable, there is no going upward, downward, or across, because He is partless and devoid of qualities.
In that [Self], which is the eternal light of pure consciousness, darkness does not exist;
how then can any effect remain for me, who am eternally liberated? (Samupad I, 14.37)
What thought can there be for one who is mindless, or what action for one who is without senses?
For "he is breathless, mindless, and pure"—this is the true word of the Veda.
Because it is timeless, placeless, directionless, and without cause, the Self has no dependence on time or other such factors for one who is constantly meditating. (Samyutta Nikaya Upadesha 1,14.39)
That mental sacred ford (mānasa-tīrtha) wherein the gods, the Vedas, and the entire purifying power attain oneness—by bathing in which one becomes immortal. (SamUpad I, 14.40)
Sound and the other [objects] do not exist as something that is not cognized by another; nor indeed are they seen even by one another.
Just as taste and the others are perceived by another, so too are bodily [sensations] perceived precisely because they are objects of perception.
The notions of "I" and "mine," as well as desire, effort, transformation, pleasure, and so forth, are seen here in this same manner;
because they possess the quality of being objects of sight, they do not themselves become the seer in relation to one another, and therefore there must be something beyond them.
For all modifications, beginning with the sense of "I-making," possess an agent and are conjoined with the fruit of action;
however, because they are illuminated on all sides by the nature of consciousness like the sun, they do not belong to the Self. (Samupad I, 14.43)
For, like space, he exists pervading the minds of all embodied beings by way of the nature of pure consciousness;
therefore, there is no other knower besides him, nor anything beyond him—thus, the Lord is one.
If the body and the intellect are seen as distinct, then the doctrines of no-self have been thoroughly refuted by me;
for the Supreme is established as stainless despite impure karma, all-pervading, untainted, and non-dual.

If the form of a jar or other objects is not perceived by you because the mind has engaged in many ways through its own functions, then the defects of impurity, insentience, and transformation inherent in the intellect cannot be avoided. (Samyutta-upadeśa 1.14.46)
Just as the pure sky is continuous, neither clinging nor being defiled, so too this Self is always equal toward all beings; for it is eternal, undecaying, immortal, and fearless.
The formless and the formed, as well as the latent impressions of karma, are imagined externally to the nature of pure seeing;
for by means of ignorance, those of deluded vision project these upon the Self, but when they are removed by the realization "not this, not this," what remains is pure seeing.
The nature of awakening, born from the mind's connection with objects, is seen as if possessing an object both in memory and in one who has slept;
likewise, due to the body being a mere reflection, both the body and the mind appear as distinct from the Seer.

Just as there is no distinction in the sky—which is pure by nature—once impurities such as clouds have vanished, so too, when the two [obstacles] have been removed by the Śruti, the vision is always undifferentiated, like the sky. (SamUpad I, 14.50)
Thus ends the section on dreams and memory. (Samyukta Āgama I.14)
Since one thing cannot become another, one should not conceive of anything as other;
for if one thing were to exist as something else, its destruction would be certain. (Samādhipradīpa I.15.1)
To one who remembers, that which was seen appears as if depicted in a painting on a cloth;
therein, those two known as the *sattva* and the *kṣetrajña* are to be understood—[the former] by whom [it is seen] and [the latter] wherein [it is seen]. (Samyukta Āgama 15.2)
Furthermore, that which has been experienced up to its fruition— being associated with the factors of action such as the agent—
and which, when being remembered, resides in the object, is therefore indeed the prior action itself.
Furthermore, for a seer, the object of sight must always be something other than himself, because it is an object of sight, like a jar;
the seer is not of the same nature as the object of sight, unlike the intellect, otherwise there would be no witness-hood.
Depending upon the cognition of its own self, this [universal] and so forth would be the motivator of injunctions;
it is like a corpse, and therefore, otherwise, there would be no plurality of selves.
Since it is said that there is neither the pleasant nor the unpleasant, the state of being bodiless is not the fruit of ritual action;
rather, connection with a body is the cause of action. Therefore, the knower should renounce actions. (Samnyāsa Upaniṣad I.15.6)

If the self is independent with regard to actions, let it likewise be accepted as such with regard to cessation. Since the state of being bodiless is a result that is not to be produced and is already known, how could one perform ritual acts?
Having completely renounced birth and the other causal signs of actions, the wise person should,
according to the scriptures, remember that essential nature which is opposed to the causes of action.
The Self alone exists in all beings, and they in It, as [the birds are] in the sky; it has pervaded everything like space, and is held to be pure and radiant. (Samyukta Upaniṣad I.15.9)
By the absence of wounds and sinews, one should ward off a gross body;
by the state of being pure and sinless, one should ward off ointment, the linga, and even the form of a body.
Just as Vāsudeva spoke of equality in the horse-fig tree and in his own body, so too he who knows the Self as equal is the best among the knowers of Brahman. (Samnyāsa Upaniṣad I.15.11)
For just as the notions of "mine" and "I" are not admitted with respect to other bodies,
so too they are not admitted with respect to this body, because there is no difference in its being the witness of the intellect.
Since passion, hatred, and fear— which are equal to the formative forces of matter—
are perceived as dependent upon the intellect, therefore the Knower is always pure and fearless.
If the mind were identical with the action, it would not attain the nature of a self;
for if the action were the self, it would be independent, whereas that [action] is not itself independent, as it depends on something else. (Samupad I.15.14)
Cognition is like space—of a single flavor, undivided, undecaying, and stainless;
yet, due to the limiting adjuncts of the eyes and other senses, it is perceived as something contrary to its true nature.
Because it is an object of perception, this notion "I" is not a property of the Self, just like a jar or other objects;
likewise, other cognitions should be understood [as non-Self], and therefore the Self is indeed stainless.
Because it is the witness of all conditions, it is unchanging and all-pervading;
if the seer were subject to modification, it would become limited in knowledge like the intellect and other faculties.

Just as the vision of the seer is not destroyed, so too [the nature] of the eye and other [senses] is not; for it has been said, "of the seer," therefore the seer is always the enjoyer. (Samyukta-upaniṣad 1.15.18)
"I am either the aggregate of the elements and likewise of the sense-faculties, or I am one or another of them individually"—thus should one investigate: "Who am I? (Samyukta Āgama 15.19).

Neither individually nor collectively is the knower either an element or a sense organ, because it is that which knows and possesses the instruments of knowledge; therefore, it is other than these, like a jar or similar objects.
The intellect is the fuel for the fire of the self; kindled by ignorance, desire, and action, it constantly blazes forth through the doors of the ears and other senses. (Samyukta Āgama 15.21)
When the intellect, ignited by the oblation of sense-objects, operates through the predominance of the right eye, then the fire of the Self is a consumer of gross food.

Remembering that "the oblations are indeed offered" during the perception of forms and other objects, one who is free from attachment and aversion is not defiled by the faults of the waking state within the fire of the Self. (Samupad I.15.23)
In the mental abode, however, the latent impressions of ignorance and karma become manifest;
seeing them, the self is called *taijasa*, illuminated by its own light. (Samyukta Upaniṣad 1.15.24)
When neither objects nor latent impressions are impelled by actions within the intellect,
then the wise one should know the Self as the Knower, for it perceives nothing else.
Those states of the mind, intellect, and senses impelled by karma are illuminated by consciousness alone, just as jars and other objects are illuminated by the sun.
This being so, the Knower, illuminating the cognitions by means of its own light, is their agent; yet it is only by the deluded that it is described as such for the sake of those [cognitions].
For this very reason, he would be omniscient, illuminating everything by his own light;
and because he is the cause of all actions, he possesses the state of being the doer of all for himself.

Thus, the Self with attributes has been described; but the Self without attributes is indefinable, partless, devoid of qualities, and pure—neither mind nor speech can reach it. (Samyukta Upaniṣad I.15.29)
Whether conscious or unconscious, an agent or a non-agent, gone or not gone, bound or liberated, likewise one or many, pure or otherwise—(so it is). 15.30.
Speech, together with the intellects, turns back indeed without having reached it,
because of its being devoid of qualities, the absence of action, and the non-existence of particularities.
Just as space is all-pervading, free from all material forms, so too should one know the self here to be pure, the supreme state. (Samādhipāda 1.32)

Having abandoned the seen, one should discard that memory along with all grasping and darkness by means of the light of universal vision, just as the sun, endowed with its radiance, dispels the night.
He whose objects of perception are the conditions that consist of the darkness regarding the recollection of form—
he alone is the Self, the equal observer, all-pervading among all beings.
From the conjunction of the self, the intellect, the mind, the eye, the object, and light,
there arises in the intellect a manifold cognition characterized by ignorance.
Having discriminated one's own self from this [body], one should know it to be pure, the supreme state—the witness abiding in all beings, equal, and transcending all fear. (SamUpad I.15.36)
It is all-encompassing, omnipresent, tranquil, stainless, and situated like the sky;
it is partless, actionless, everything, eternal, and devoid of dualities.
"How can I, who am the knower and witness of all objects of knowledge, know [Brahman]?"—having reflected thus, one should discern whether Brahman has been known or not. (Samnyāsa Upaniṣad 1.15.38)
"Because of scriptural injunctions such as 'the unseen seer' and 'the unknown,' the supreme Brahman cannot be known by me or by others in any way whatsoever. (Samupad I, 15.39)
Because it is not separated from its own nature, because its essence is the light of knowledge,
and because it does not depend on another cognition, it is indeed always known by me.
The sun has no need for another light to illuminate itself;
likewise, consciousness has no desire for another consciousness to illuminate it, for it illuminates itself by its own nature.
That which constitutes the very nature of a thing does not depend on anything else;
for there is no manifestation whatsoever that is perceivable by another manifestation. (Samupad I.15.42)
The manifestation of that which was unmanifest occurs through union with the nature of light;
yet to say that light itself is the effect of the sun is indeed a false statement. (Samupad I, 15.43)
Whatever comes into being after not having existed is accepted as its effect;
however, because it is his very nature, the light of the sun does not arise after having not existed.

Just as the sun and other luminaries are accepted as the makers of light merely by their existence, so too should it be accepted for that whose nature is consciousness, in contrast to the manifestation of objects such as jars. 15.45.
Just as the sun is illuminating when it emerges from behind a cloud,
so too is the knower of the self luminous by its very nature of consciousness, without any effort.
Just as fire is hot when it exists, so too should it be understood in the case of the conscious self;
for [the appearance of duality] arises only when the limiting adjunct (upādhi) is present, like a snake that has emerged from a rope. (SamUpad I, 15.47)
Just like that, even though the Knower is effortless, the Knower would be an agent like a turner;
therefore, the Self is neither knowable by its own nature nor unknowable.
Because of the teaching that it is something entirely other than both the known and the unknown,
states such as bondage and liberation are likewise imagined in the self.
Just as there is no distinction between day and night in the sun due to the lack of difference in its luminous form, so too,
because of the lack of difference in the nature of consciousness, there is neither consciousness nor unconsciousness in the Self.
As it has been said: "He who knows Brahman as devoid of rejection and acquisition, according to the prescribed method, is truly not born again. (Samyuktopaniṣad I.15.51)
One who has fallen into the currents of birth and death would not be able to lift oneself out of this state by any means other than knowledge. (Samyukta Upaniṣad I, 15.52)
“The knot of the heart is severed, all doubts are cut away, and his karmas are exhausted—when He is seen,” so says the Śruti. (SamUpad I.15.53)

Having completely cast off the notions of "mine" and "I," the state that is like the sky and from which the body is liberated is proclaimed through well-observed scripture and inference; if a person is certain of this, they are released.
Thus ends the chapter on "Neither One Nor Another. 1.15.
The solid element in the body is known as earth; the liquid is considered to be water;
and digestion, movement, and space arise from fire, air, and ether, respectively. 16.1.

The olfactory and other sense organs, as well as their respective objects—the qualities of earth and so forth—are held to be of the same class [as their objects], just like color and light. (SamUpad I.16.2)
They say that these [organs], speech, hands, and so forth, exist for the sake of cognition and action;
the internal mind, which serves to differentiate them, is the eleventh.
The intellect should be of the nature of certainty; it is that which experiences all objects. The Knower of the Self is said to be always manifesting by means of its own luminous nature.
Just as light, having assumed the form of the object manifested by it, remains unmixed even when intermingled [with other objects], so too the Knower is always unmixed with the cognitions. 16.5.
Just as a lamp that stands without effort illuminates everything it reaches,
so too the Knower perceives the cognitions that have reached him in the forms of sound and other objects.
Pleasure and the like qualify the cognition— which has taken the aggregate of body and senses as its object through the notion of "self"— as being illumined by the light of the eternal Self.
For one perceives oneself as "I am suffering" due to headaches and the like;
yet the seer is other than the suffering object of sight, and because he is the seer, he is not the sufferer.
One would be miserable either through the conceit "I am miserable" or from seeing others who are miserable;
yet the seer, being a composite of limbs and so forth, is not at all miserable in relation to suffering.

If the eye were both the agent and the object of action like the visual faculty itself, it would not be a single entity; moreover, being a composite, it could not be the self, for that which is the seer cannot become the object of seeing. (Samyukta Āgama, I.16.10)
If it is held that the self also possesses multiplicity, such as knowledge, effort, and so forth, [we reply]:
because it has the single quality of consciousness, it cannot be an object of action, like light. (Samupad I.16.11)

Just as light, despite its illuminating nature, does not illuminate itself, so too, even though there is a distinction [between the knower and the known], the knowing Self does not perceive itself, because of their equality. 16.12.
A thing cannot become the object of its own nature;
for fire does not burn itself, nor does it illuminate itself in that way. (Samyukta-avakara-pada 16.13)
By this very [argument], the grasping of the self by the self through the intellect is refuted;
for even a part is not tenable, because it would be equal [to the whole] and thus lack distinction. (Samupad I.16.14)

Even emptiness is not tenable in this way, because it would have to be perceived by something other than cognition; for that reason, like a jar, its existence prior [to cognition] is established through conceptual construction.
That non-conceptual [reality] certainly exists, which previously existed through conceptualization;
for it is the cause of the arising of conceptualization, and it alone is its cause.
Ignorance is the root of conceptualization and the regulator of saṃsāra;
having abandoned [the notion of] the self, one should know the Supreme Brahman as eternally liberated and fearless. (Samupad I.16.17)
Waking and dreaming are the seeds of that state called deep sleep, which consists of darkness;
because they do not exist within one another, one should abandon these three as being non-existent.
Due to the confusion of the self, intellect, mind, eye, light, objects, and so forth,
there arises the delusion that "the action is the self," resulting from the conjunction of these activities.
The closing and opening [of the eyes] belong to the wind element and do not pertain to the eye;
likewise, because of its luminosity, these two do not exist in the mind or in the intellect, since they are manifestations of light.
Volition and determination belong respectively to the mind and the intellect;
they do not possess each other's attributes, and all [of these] are imagined within the Self. (Samupad I.16.21)
The vision of the senses would be limited to their respective locations;
for the intellect, having attained identity with them, perceives that [object] and appears as if it were merely the body. (Samupad I.16.22)
For that is indeed momentary, consisting of nothing but dharmas in uninterrupted succession;
due to similarity, it is perceived as a single entity like a lamp-flame, and its cessation is the goal of human endeavor. (Samupad I.16.23)

For those for whom form and so forth exist as having their own specific forms and as appearing as something else, and for whom there is nothing other than that, the aforementioned inconsistency is stated. *Samuccaya-pañjikā* I, 16.24.
Because cognition possesses an external form, there is always an absence of memory due to its momentariness;
and because of its momentariness, the intellect never deposits any latent impression (*saṃskāra*) anywhere.
Furthermore, because the substratum itself is non-existent, there would be equality due to the absence of a cause;
or, if it were to remain, there would be a loss of momentariness, which is not accepted.
Since peace is accomplished without effort, the statement of its means is purposeless;
because peace is complete in each [moment], it has no dependence on anything else. (SamUpad I, 16.27)
If dependence is admitted even toward a distinct continuum belonging to another,
then since all things are momentary, there would likewise be a lack of dependence on anything else.
Arising simultaneously and joined with one another, that which is conditioned by their conjunction is capable of perceiving the other. (Samyukta Āgama 16.29)
But where there is false superimposition, the destruction of that [superimposition] is our view;
tell me, for whom would liberation be the fruit if it were the destruction of everything? (Samupad I, 16.30)
Whether that which is called "self" is indeed cognition, or something else entirely,
its non-existence cannot be established, because it is known through both existence and non-existence.
If that by which non-existence is apprehended were itself not to exist,
then there would be a lack of knowledge regarding both existence and non-existence on the part of the world, which is not accepted.

That which is intended prior to the conceptual constructions of "existent," "non-existent," and "both existent and non-existent" is non-duality; because it is equal [to all], it is eternal and distinct from that which is conceptually constructed. 16.33.

Because it arises from conceptual construction, let duality be regarded as non-existent, like a dream-object; for it was non-existent prior [to that construction], and because of the conceptualization of its existence, non-existence, and so forth.

And because of the scriptural teaching that modifications are merely a matter of verbal designation, and because of such [scriptural] passages as "From death to death he goes" and the Smṛti statement "This world is My Māyā," modifications are indeed non-existent. // SamUpad I.16.35 //
And for this very reason, its purity is distinct from conceptual construction; therefore, the self, not imagined by others, is to be accepted and not rejected. (SamUpad I.16.36)
Just as there is no lack of light in the sun by its very nature as light,
so too there is no ignorance in the Self because its essential nature is eternal consciousness.
Likewise, because its nature is changeless, there is no other state for the Self;
for if it were to possess another state, it would undoubtedly undergo destruction.
For one for whom liberation is a distinct state produced by effort, it is indeed transitory;
therefore, liberation can in no way be logically conceived as either conjunction or disjunction.
Because conjunction is impermanent and likewise disjunction,
as well as going and coming, its essential nature does not perish.
Because its own nature (svarūpa) is not a cause, whereas other [factors] are indeed possessed of causes;
for its own nature is neither acquired by it nor abandoned by itself. (SamUpad I, 16.41)

Because it is the very nature of all things, it cannot be abandoned, for it is non-different from them; nor can it be grasped, because it is eternal, beyond the reach of the senses, and not distinct [from reality].
And because everything has the self as its ultimate purpose, the self alone is eternal;
therefore, the knower of liberation should renounce all ritual actions along with their means. (Samyukta Upaniṣad I.16.43)
"The attainment of the Self is the supreme attainment"—such are the scriptural authorities and logical proofs.
The attainment of anything other than the Self is a non-attainment; therefore, one should abandon the notion of non-Selfhood. (Samyukta Āgama I, 16.44)
Indeed, the loss of the equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas) is not possible;
nor is any other cause admitted, because ignorance and the rest remain dormant. (Samādhipādādhikāra 1.45)
If they were mutually causal, activity would either occur constantly or not at all;
there would be no restriction regarding the activities within the *guṇas* or within the Self (*ātman*).
The distinction between those who are liberated and those who are bound is not tenable if both have that [Brahman] as their sole purpose;
nor is the relationship between the object and the seeker of the object possible, for neither the knower nor the other is a seeker of an object.

Furthermore, the subservience of primordial matter (pradhāna) to another is not logical even according to the Sāṃkhya treatise, because the person (puruṣa) is changeless; nor is it logical even if [the person] were subject to modification.

Furthermore, because no relationship between primordial matter (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa) is possible, it is illogical for the primary matter to exist for the sake of that [person], since it is insentient. (Samkhyakārikā 59)
If [the cause] perishes upon the arising of the effect, it is the same as in the case of mere cognition;
however, if it were without a cause, the consequence would be that liberation from Pradhāna is impossible.
Just as heat cannot be made manifest by cognition itself, so too pleasure and the like cannot be grasped by it;
for those who follow the path of Kaṇāda and others, these would be ungraspable due to their residing in the same locus.
Furthermore, because pleasure and cognition cannot exist simultaneously, and because pleasure has the same cause as mental contact, pleasure itself is ungraspable. (Samyuktabhidharmahṛdaya 16.52)
Likewise, because other [qualities] are distinct, simultaneous production is not accepted;
if it is argued that the inherence of qualities is cognition, it is not so, because of the lack of distinction.
Because it is qualified by cognition alone, memory likewise has cognition as its object;
for [memory] consists of the form "happiness was known by me," since its nature is that of non-cognition (ajñāna).

Pleasure and the like cannot be attributes of the self, because for you the self is immutable; nor can they belong to something else, because that would involve a distinction, and why not to the mind as well, since there is no difference [in its being distinct from the self]?
But if knowledge were to become an object of cognition, it would either be like a garland that must be avoided, or else,
if simultaneous production is accepted, a logical extreme (anta) is reached.
Furthermore, because there is no other state of existence, bondage does not exist in the Self;
nor is there impurity, because of its non-attachment, as the Śruti declares: "For it is unattached. (Samupad I, 16.57)
And because of the scriptural statement, "It is not tainted by those things that are subtle and within the range of the one," if this were so,
then there would be no liberation whatsoever, due to the absence of bondage.
In this way, the treatises would be rendered useless; nor is the error of the intellect admitted [as the cause].
Bondage and liberation are its destruction; it is as has been stated, and not otherwise. (Samupad I,16.59)
Illumined by the light of the self which is awakening, the intellect conceives of awakening within itself;
that "there is no other knower" is indeed this delusion residing in the intellect. (Samupad I, 16.60)
Since consciousness is the very nature of the Self, it is metaphorically designated as eternal therein;
this beginningless non-discrimination is held to be nothing other than saṃsāra itself.
Liberation must be the very destruction of that [bondage], for it cannot be established otherwise;
for those for whom liberation is the attainment of another entity, destruction is what they consider to be liberation.
In this way, even a change of state is not tenable for that which is unchanging;
if there were change, it would possess the nature of a composite whole, and consequently, its destruction would follow, as in the case of a jar or similar objects.

Therefore, all other conceptual constructions regarding bondage, liberation, and so forth— those of the Sāṃkhyas, the Kāṇādas, and the Buddhists— are indeed errors, their constructs shattered by Mīmāṃsā.
Because they contradict scripture and reasoning, they should never be respected;
their faults can be stated by the hundreds and thousands. (Samyutta-upadeśa I, 16.65)

Furthermore, because of the occurrence of censure [regarding other systems], and because of the phrase "and those others besides this," the wise person should abandon the teachings of other scriptures and form a firm conviction in this one. (Samupad I, 16.66)
Placing faith and devotion foremost, and abandoning all insincerity, [one should apply oneself] to the true meaning of the Vedānta and likewise to the thought of Vyāsa. (SamUpad I, 16.67)

Thus, the conceptualization of dualistic discourse and the doctrines of selflessness have been refuted through reasoning; so that those seeking liberation, free from doubt regarding the arguments of others, may remain steadfast on the path of knowledge.

Having correctly attained that self-witnessing knowledge—which is exceedingly pure, contrary to conceptual constructions, and non-dual—if one becomes firmly certain, one attains the eternal nirvāṇa without remainder. (Samādhipradīpa I, 16.69)

This is the supreme secret, the ultimate refuge; having discerned it, those who are free from defects and devoid of pride should always direct their intellect toward uprightness, for no one possesses true vision who holds a mind fixed on their own [limited] views.

By means of this supreme purifier, a person is liberated from the sins accumulated over many previous births which have ignorance as their cause; having realized this, one is not smeared by actions here, just like the sky. (Samyukta Upanishad I.16.71)

This should always be given to one whose mind is tranquil, who has conquered the senses, who has abandoned faults, who acts according to what has been taught, who is endowed with virtues, who is ever-devoted, and who seeks liberation. (Samayupad I, 16.72)
Just as there is no sense of "I" regarding the body of another, so it is when one perceives the ultimate reality;
for having attained this exceedingly pure knowledge, one then becomes liberated from everything. (Samyukta Upaniṣad I.16.73)
For there is no gain here whatsoever that exceeds the attainment of one's true nature; for this is obtained from this [nature] alone and not from anything else.
One should not give away the attainment of one's true nature—even an empire greater than Indra's—without first examining it with great effort.
Thus ends the section on the earthly [elements]. (Samyukta-upadeśa I.16)
The Self is to be known as the supreme Self, from which nothing else exists; it is all-knowing, all-seeing, and pure. Homage to that Self, who is the object of knowledge! (Samupad I.17.1)
I perpetually bow down to those who, being experts in grammar, logic, and epistemology, have illuminated the Brahman— the secret of the Vedas— acting as lamps.

Or rather, having bowed to those gurus by whose speech the impurity of darkness is destroyed through the falling of the sun's rays, I shall declare the definitive determination of the knowledge of Brahman. (SamUpad I, 17.3)
There is no gain whatsoever superior to the attainment of the Self;
for that purpose alone exist the declarations of the Vedas as well as the ritual acts prescribed in the Smṛtis.

For even that gain which is for one's own sake is desired for the sake of pleasure, yet its opposite is the supreme attainment of the Self (ātmalābha), so it is declared by the knowers of Brahman because of its eternity. (Samyukta Upaniṣad I.17.5)
Because its own nature is self-attained, its acquisition does not come from anything else;
however, that acquisition which depends on another arises from the vision of another.
Ignorance, however, would be any other view; its destruction is called liberation.
That too must occur through knowledge alone, because of its opposition [to ignorance], and not through action. (Samupad I.17.7)
But the effect of karma is impermanent, having ignorance and desire as its causes;
in this matter, the Veda alone is traditionally held to be the authority for the attainment of knowledge.
Because it is devoted to a single object of knowledge, they know that sentence to be one;
for the oneness of the Self is to be understood through the comprehension of the meaning of the sentence. (Samyutta-upaniṣad I.17.9)
However, the distinction between them is to be inferred from the difference in their designations; for they too are denoted by those very terms.
Therefore, this triad is proclaimed as form, name, and action. (Samupad I.17.10)
Therefore, this triad is non-existent, for it is indeed mutually imagined;
just as a color is produced from a sound heard elsewhere by the intellect as something external.
Just as a form seen by the intellect is conceptualized as sound,
so too is this entire world conceptualized by the deluded intellect.
Therefore, that [duality] is unreal; what is real is only pure consciousness, which is not imagined.
That very same [consciousness] is the primordial Veda, while anything else that is known is imagined.
That by which one knows is the Veda; everything in a dream, however, is through illusion (māyā).
That by which one sees is the eye; that by which one hears is called the ear. (Samupad I.17.14)
That by which one speaks while dreaming is speech, and likewise the sense of smell, as well as taste and touch, the mind, and the other sense organs. (Samyukta Āgama Upadeśa 1.17.15)
This single cognition appears divided in many ways solely through imagined limiting adjuncts;
just as the division of a single gem arises from the difference in its settings.
Likewise, for one who is awake, this differentiation of knowledge is conceptualized;
driven by the activity arising from craving, one explains the object as residing within the intellect through delusion.

Just as it is in a dream and likewise upon waking, both externally and internally, so too is it like the viewing of a painting or the study of a text—arising from the mutual cognition of one another. (SamUpad I.17.18)
When he conceives a distinction, being desirous of that according to his resolve—
having become one whose resolve is directed toward whatever he desires— he attains that which has been performed.
This entire world is unreal, for it originates from ignorance;
since it is perceived by one who possesses that ignorance, yet is not grasped in deep sleep. (Samyukta Upaniṣad I.17.20)
For us, knowledge and ignorance as declared in the scriptures consist indeed in the cognitions of unity and difference;
therefore, with every effort, knowledge is enjoined in the sacred teaching. (Samupad I.17.21)
For when the mind is pure like a mirror, knowledge shines forth; its purification is achieved through constant restraints, sacrifices, and austerities. (Samyukta Upaniṣads I.17.22)

One should perform the highest austerity, such as that of the body and so forth, for the sake of purifying it; this consists of the concentration of the mind and other faculties, as well as the emaciation of those respective bodies. (Samupad I, 17.23)

One should know that which is seen as the waking state, and that very same thing when remembered as the dream state; and the non-existence of those two is deep sleep—one's own Self, the supreme state. (Samyukta Upaniṣad 1.17.24)
The darkness of ignorance called deep sleep is the seed of dreaming and waking;
when scorched by the awakening to one's own Self, that seed becomes like a burnt seed, no longer capable of sprouting.
That very same single seed of *māyā* should again be understood as threefold in sequence:
although the Self is changeless and one, it appears manifold like the sun reflected in water.
Just as a single seed is divided by means of sprouts, dreams, and so forth,
so too is the Self [divided] within the bodies of dreaming and waking, like the reflection of the moon in water.
Just as a magician might travel alone after mounting an illusory elephant,
so too the Self— though immovable— appears to come and go when it presides over the vital breaths, dreams, and other states.
Just as there is neither the elephant nor the one mounted upon it, but rather another who stands as the magician;
so too there are neither the vital breaths and the rest, nor the observer of them, but rather the Knower, who is eternally the Seer.
For one whose eyes are not bound, there is no illusion, nor even for the illusionist;
that illusion belongs only to the one whose eyes are bound, and therefore it becomes the illusionist himself.

He is to be known as directly manifest, for the Śruti declares, "He is the directly manifest Self," and because of the Śruti beginning with, "The knot of the heart is severed, if... (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.8).

Since it does not consist of sound and the other [sense objects], its apprehension could not occur through the sense faculties; likewise, since it is distinct from pleasure and the like, how could it be apprehended by the intellect either? (Samupad I, 17.32)
Just as Rāhu, though invisible, [is perceived] in the moon, and as a reflection [is seen] in water,
so too the Self, though omnipresent, is apprehended only in the awakened mind.
Just as the orb of the sun and its heat are seen in water but do not belong to the water,
so too consciousness exists in the intellect but is not a property of it, because their natures are different.

Perceiving that activity of the intellect which is joined with the eye, the Self—whose vision is unimpaired—is the seer of seeing; likewise, it is the hearer of hearing and the hearer of what is heard.
Perceiving the activity of the mind alone, the unborn thinker [remains] as the knower because his power of cognition is never lost; therefore, the scripture says "not so" (na hi). 17.36.
"‘It meditates’ indicates its immutability; likewise, ‘it moves about’ indicates its activity. Here, ‘the thief’ indicates its purity, as the scripture states it is ‘unattached. (SamUpad I.17.37)
Because its power is not lost, the Knower remains as such even in deep sleep; likewise, it is unchanged in the state of waking.
However, according to the view of the Śruti, there is a distinction only in the objects of knowledge, wherever they may arise.
For the non-Self is remote from the worldly vision due to being veiled;
but because the vision has the nature of the Self, that Brahman is remembered as being directly perceived. (Samupad I, 17.39)
Just as there is no dependence on another lamp for the illumination of a lamp, so too, because consciousness is the very nature of the self, no other consciousness is required. (Samupad I.17.40)
For the Self is not admitted to be an object, nor subject to modification, nor manifold;
therefore, it is neither to be abandoned nor to be acquired, either by another or by itself.
He who knows, "I am the Self, undecaying within and without, transcending birth, death, and old age"—from what indeed could he fear? (Samyukta Upanishad I.17.42)
Even prior to this [instruction], action is excluded by the removal of qualities such as being of a particular caste;
for that [Self] is determined from scriptures such as "not gross" and so forth, as well as from the statement "That thou art. (Samupad I.17.43)
Because birth and the other characteristics are abandoned upon the relinquishment of the previous body, birth and so forth belong to the body alone; thus, even that [body] is likewise without self.

Therefore, ignorance regarding the body and other non-self entities—consisting of the notions "mine" and "I"—is to be abandoned through the knowledge of the Self, according to the Śruti: "This belongs to the Asuras. (Samupad I.17.45)

Just as [the duties] upon the attainment of knowledge cease for one who has entered the wandering life (pārivrājya), so too do the rites pertaining to birth and other [life-cycle events], such as those involving the ten-day period of impurity, cease. 17.46.
Having become the very intention of whatever one desires, the ignorant person attains what has been done;
but when the desires of one who sees his own Self are liberated, then he becomes immortal.
The purpose of the injunction regarding the nature of the Self is the turning away from action and the like;
for according to scripture, the Self is not something to be accomplished nor a means of accomplishment, being eternally satisfied.
The fruit of action consists of that which is to be produced, that which is not subject to modification, and that which is to be refined;
there is no other effect of action than these. Therefore, one should abandon action along with its means.

Because it ends in suffering, because it is impermanent, and because it does not serve the self, one who seeks the truth should withdraw that external delight into the self and take refuge in a teacher.

"One who is peaceful, wise, likewise liberated, inactive, and established in Brahman—through scripture and through the traditional teaching that 'one who has a teacher knows it,' one should know that [Brahman] to be thus. (Samyukta Upanishad I.17.51)

That guru shall swiftly ferry across, by means of the raft of the knowledge of Brahman, the disciple who is disciplined and endowed with the qualities of a disciple, [across] the great ocean of darkness within his own mind.

Vision, touch, hearing, smell, thought, and even discernment—these and other powers are differentiated by limiting adjuncts (upādhi), even though they are of the nature of consciousness. (Samupad I, 17.53)
Free from rebirth in the lower realms and shining eternally like the sun, he is all-pervading, all-seeing, and pure; he knows everything at all times.
One who holds another view [thinks]: "The Self, residing in the body, is indeed limited by that much due to ignorance;
yet, through similes such as the moon in water and so forth, it is conceived as possessing those [reflected] attributes. (Samyukta Āgama Upadeśa I, 17.55)
Having seen the external, one should then close [the eyes]; having remembered that, one should abandon it;
then, opening one's own vision, one attains Brahman without traveling on a path.
Having thus abandoned this triad beginning with *prāṇa*, he has crossed the great ocean of ignorance;
established in his own self, devoid of qualities, pure, awakened, he is indeed liberated by himself. (Samupad I, 17.57)
"I am unborn, immortal, deathless, ageless, and indeed fearless;
omniscient, all-seeing, and pure"—one who has awakened thus is not born again. (Samādhipradīpa-sūtra 1.17.58)
It is certain that the seed of darkness previously mentioned does not exist;
in its absence, how can there be birth for one who realizes the oneness of Brahman? (Samyukta Upaniṣad I.17.59)
