Just as butter, having been extracted from milk, is no longer the same once it has been cast back into it, so too the knower, being unreal apart from intellect and the rest, the embodied self would not be as it was before. 17.60.
"I am Truth, Knowledge, and Infinity, beyond the five elements beginning with taste;
I am that which is described in the scriptures as invisible and so forth—I am Brahman," thus one should remain fearless.
Since speech, mind, fire, and the other [senses] proceed out of fear, he who knows the reality of the bliss of the Self does not fear anything whatsoever. (Samupad I, 17.62)

If one who knows the Self is established in the non-dual plenitude, the sovereign state that transcends name and the rest, then whom should he bow to? At that time, no ritual action remains to be performed.
The Virāj Vaiśvānara is the external [self], while the one who remembers within is Prajāpati;
but when everything has dissolved, the wise one is called the Undifferentiated (avyākṛta).
Since the triad beginning with deep sleep consists of nothing more than a verbal handle, it is unreal;
one who is firm in truth is liberated by realizing, "I am the true Knower. (Samupad I.17.65)
Just as for the sun, because it is of the nature of light, there is neither day nor night,
so too for me there can be neither knowledge nor ignorance, since there is no distinction in my being of the nature of consciousness.
Because the teaching is beyond doubt, one should reflect: "I shall always be Brahman itself;
for me, who am Brahman, there is nothing to be abandoned nor anything to be grasped. (SamUpad I, 17.67)
I alone am one among all beings, like the sky;
seeing all beings in me, one is not born again. (Samyukta Upanishad I.17.68)
Nothing other exists externally, in the middle, or internally, nor anywhere by itself;
because there is no hearing of anything external or internal, it is therefore pure and self-luminous.
From scriptures such as "not this, not this," [reality is] the cessation of phenomenal proliferation and non-dual;
and from scriptures such as "the unknown," it is indeed not to be known otherwise than in this way. (SamUpad I, 17.70)
If the supreme Brahman is known as "I alone am the Self of all," then that is the Self of all beings, for the Śruti declares: "He is indeed the Self of these. (SamUpad I.17.71)
If the individual soul (jīva) directly perceives the Supreme Self as his own self,
the God who is to be worshipped by the gods, he turns away from the state of being a beast for the gods.
"I alone am the knower of the Real, while others are void like the sky"—
because of such commitment to truth, the one who perceives the unreal is not bound.
Those who know Brahman otherwise than this are indeed pitiable;
for the gods are under the control of that self-ruling one who, established in himself, perceives nothing else.
Having abandoned the connection with birth and so forth, as well as other words along with their corresponding actions,
take refuge in your own entire, pure Self by means of the syllable "Om" alone.
The bridge of all established orders, devoid of day and night and the like,
extending horizontally, upwards, and downwards— everything is at once light, free from affliction.
One should know one's own self as distinct from merit and demerit, from the past and the future, and from the done and the undone; it is liberated from all bonds. (Samyukta Āgama Upadeśa 1.17.77)
Not acting, yet performing all, pure, he stands transcending those who run;
through his illusory power (*māyā*) and omnipotence, being unborn, he is conceived as manifold. (Samupad I, 17.78)
Like a king, because I am merely a witness; like a magnet, because of my proximity—I, the Self, while causing the world to revolve, am actionless, a non-doer, and non-dual. (Samupad I,17.79)

One should maintain the realization: "I am that Brahman which is devoid of qualities, actionless, eternal, free from dualities, and without affliction; pure, awakened, and likewise liberated. (Samyukta Upaniṣad I.17.80)

Having understood exactly as it is this one pure reality— the supreme truth that transcends both the knowable and the unknowable, which is beyond both bondage and liberation, and wherein both this single and this dual are to be abandoned—
one transcends sorrow and delusion, as declared by the Śrutis and the Munis.
The Brāhmaṇa who has attained his task becomes all-knowing, the doer of all, and free from the fear of worldly existence.

"One's own self is not to be abandoned by oneself, nor is another's; likewise, one's own self is not to be accepted, nor is that of another. Such is the right understanding (samyagmati). — *Samādhipradīpa* I, 17.82.
For this [knowledge], which is the domain of all Vedāntas, is that by which one gains conviction regarding the Self;
indeed, having known it, people are liberated from all the bonds of saṃsāra. (Samupad I, 17.83)
This secret of all the Vedas and even of the gods,
which is the supreme and most purifying— this very thing has now been fully revealed.
This supreme secret knowledge is not to be given to one who is not tranquil;
it should be bestowed upon a disciple who is dispassionate and devoted.
And for one who imparts knowledge to himself, no other [agent] exists that is devoid of action;
therefore, one who desires knowledge should always be disciplined with the qualities of a disciple.
Since there exists nothing other than knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the knower,
homage to Him who is the essence of knowledge, the omniscient, and the omnipotent.
Homage to those omniscient teachers, by whose knowledge we have been delivered from the great ocean of birth and death, which is filled with ignorance. (SamUpad I, 17.88)
Thus ends the section on Right Understanding. Samyukta Āgama I, 17.
Salutation to that Self, whose nature is the cognition of the intellect, by which the mental modifications dissolve and arise, for the sake of eternal realization. (Samupad I.18.1)

Having crushed the enemy of the Vedas hundreds of times with the sword-like words of scripture, fortified by diamond-like arguments, the one of vast intellect protected the treasure-trove of the Vedic meaning; salutations to that Lord of Ascetics, the most venerable teacher.
If the conviction "I am indeed eternally liberated, I am Being alone" does not arise in this way, for what purpose would the revered Śruti proclaim it thus like a mother? 18.3.

Precisely because of this established fact that "I am," your notion of a self is negated through reasoning by means of the teachings such as "That thou art," just as the notion of a snake in a rope is [negated]. (Samupad I, 18.4)
The existence of phenomena such as merit and so forth is to be known through the authority of the scriptures;
just as poison is dispelled by meditation, so too shall there be the removal of evil.
The two cognitions, "I am the real Brahman" and "I am performing [actions]," are both witnessed by the Self;
of these two, the abandonment of that which is born of ignorance alone is considered more appropriate.

The cognition arising from a means of valid knowledge that "I exist" is sublated by another cognition arising from something resembling it—whether resembling perception or other means—just like the delusion of directions and the like. (SamUpad I.18.7)
The scriptural teaching that there is an agent and an enjoyer merely conforms to the common understanding of the world;
this notion is sublated by the other cognition arising from the Vedic revelation: "I am Being. (Samupad I, 18.8)

When it is said, "You are indeed Being," one does not immediately attain a firm conviction regarding the liberation of the Self; therefore, one should reflect upon this through reasoning. (SamUpad I, 18.9)

Even one who understands the meaning of a sentence may not grasp it when it is stated only once; for that very reason, we have stated another [requirement], for those two are indeed required. (SamUpad I.18.10)

Since the [true nature of] actions has not been realized, that application (niyoga) may exist as long as it remains non-contradictory, until the realization [of that nature] becomes firm. (Samupad I.18.11)
And likewise, one acts falsely according to one's own whims; therefore, discernment must be practiced as long as the Self is not directly experienced. (Samyukta-upaniṣad 1.18.12)

The cognition "I am" arising from the senses certainly sublates [the notion of selflessness]; moreover, one who possesses firm latent impressions is drawn outward by defects produced by words. (Samupad I, 18.13)
Since the two types of cognition arising from scripture and inference have universals as their objects,
the sense-born [perception] must necessarily exclude them in order to have a particular as its object.
No one who realizes the meaning of a sentence is found to be free from suffering;
nor, if anyone were seen [to be so], it would be merely by hearing the meaning of the sentence. (Samādhipradīpa 18.15)
That he was free from suffering in past bodies and had cultivated his being is inferred;
if that were so, our conduct would not be perceptible by those who do not know the scriptures, and that would be undesirable.
Having stated the fruit with the words "Thou art Being," the means [to that end] must be prescribed;
for nothing other than *prasaṃkhyāna* (contemplative discernment) is accepted here as the established means.
Therefore, one who possesses tranquility and the like should strive with effort for direct experience itself, abandoning that which is contrary to the means and their goal. 18.18.
This is not so, because the secrets [of the Vedanta] culminate in "not this, not this" (neti neti);
for that which is to be accomplished through action was taught in the past, whereas liberation is eternally established.
Just as the suffering of a son is superimposed by the father upon his own self which is not suffering,
so too is it superimposed by the agent of "I" (ahaṃkartṛ) upon its own self which is eternally free from suffering.

That superimposition is negated by the [scriptural statement] "not this, not this" once it has been established; no further injunction for superimposition can possibly arise from any source whatsoever.
Just as here [in this world] there is superimposition upon the Self and likewise its negation,
so too are the superimposition of impurity and its negation performed in the sky by the ignorant.
If liberation were already attained and then prohibited, it would certainly be impermanent;
therefore, this is a prohibition of what has not been attained, like the [prohibition against] piling up a divine fire-altar and so forth.
A word or a cognition is possible within its proper domain, and not otherwise;
likewise, the "I-maker" (ahaṃkartṛ) and that [Self] are not possible [as distinct entities], because they are of the same nature. (Samupad I.18.24)
Whatever agency and other such qualities are attributed to the conscious Self by means of the ego-sense,
all that— along with the ego-sense— is negated by the teaching "not this, not this."

Apprehension, self-luminous, the Seer, directly perceptible and inactive, manifest, the innermost of all, the Witness, consciousness, eternal, devoid of qualities, and non-dual. (Samnyāsa Upaniṣad I, 18.26)
In its constant proximity, there would arise a conceit consisting of the appearance of that [mind];
from this, the duality of self and what belongs to the self would become the objective domain of "I" and "mine. (Samupad I, 18.27)
For because it possesses genus, action, and so forth, words indeed function as the ego-sense (ahaṃkṛti) toward that [body];
no word whatsoever functions toward one's own self, because of the absence of those [qualities] there.
Wherever there is an appearance, it is there that words, residing in the inward-looking vision, may indicate [the Self];
they can never directly denote it. (Samupad I.18.29)
For no object whatsoever possessing birthlessness and so forth is defined by words;
since the ego-sense (*ahaṃkṛt*) appears as the self, it is thus expressed by words such as "self. (SamUpad I.18.30)
Just as fire-logs and the like serve the purpose of fire because they exist for the sake of another and not directly [as fire],
so too the reflection of a face is other than the face itself, appearing as such through its conformity with the mirror.

Just as a face appears [in a mirror] by following the reflection due to the proximity of the mirror, so too the appearance of a self through the activity of ego-grasping is held to be like the appearance of a face. *Samādhirāja-upadeśa* I.18.32.
The Self stands like the face, and those two [the reflection and the face] remain likewise undistinguished;
that which is the ego-sense (ahaṃkṛti) is the single appearance that constitutes the transmigrating being.

Others hold that the object, its reflection, a cause other than memory such as sweetness and so forth, a portion of the knower, or a modification, serves as the substratum for those appearances. *Samādhipādopadeśa* I.18.34.

Some maintain that the transmigrating being is the ego-maker (*ahaṃkartṛ*) itself, acting independently; others hold that the transmigrating being is the continuum of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) and so forth, and not a separate, persisting entity. *Samayapaddhati* I, 18.35.
Thus have the followers of the Sugata spoken; let the logic therein be examined.
Let the discussion regarding transmigrating beings be set aside for now, and what is relevant to the present topic shall be stated.
The appearance of a face in a mirror is a phenomenon that belongs to neither [of the two];
if it were a property of one of the two, it would exist even when separated from the other. (SamUpad I, 18.37)
If it is thought that [the reflection] belongs to the face alone because it is designated by means of the face, [we reply:
no, because it conforms to the mirror and because it is not perceived when the face is present [elsewhere]. (SamUpad I.18.38)
If it is argued that [the perception occurs] only for two [of them], that is not so, because even for those two, [the object] is not seen;
for one who is unseen, there would be a perception of Rāhu in relation to the moon and the sun.
The substantiality of Rāhu is established even prior [to this discussion] by means of scriptural authority;
however, in the view that it is a shadow, its lack of substantiality would follow from the previous reasoning.
This is a negation of being overtaken by a shadow, but it does not establish [the existence of] substantial reality;
for a sentence directed toward one object cannot express another object. (Samupad I.18.41)

Furthermore, effects such as sweetness [resulting] from the non-consumption of hot substances and so forth belong to shade; this is not due to an unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), because it is observed in water itself. (SamUpad I, 18.42)
And just as the reflection of a face has the reflection as its basis, so too the appearance of a self has the reflection as its basis;
furthermore, the non-existence of these appearances is understood through both scripture and reasoning. (Samupad I.18.43)
Since the Seer (dṛśi) is unchanging, since the appearance (ābhāsa) is unreal,
and since the ego-maker (ahaṃkartṛ) is unconscious, to whom could there be the state of transmigratory existence?
Therefore, let transmigratory existence be merely ignorance due to a lack of discrimination;
it is eternally possessed of a Self by means of the immutable Self, as if it were the Self itself. (Samkhyakārikābhāṣya 1.18.45)

Just as a rope-snake appears to possess a self due to the rope prior to discrimination, so too does this [universe], though non-existent in reality, appear through the immutable Self. (Samupad I, 18.46)

Some maintain that the self, which is the substratum for the appearance of a self, undergoes modification through its own conditions; thus it is happy, miserable, a transmigrating being, and yet eternally so. (Samyukta Āgama, I, 18.47)

Due to their failure to fully understand the appearance of the self, those who lack scriptural authority are deluded regarding its true nature and imagine the agent of the "I" to be the self. (Samyukta-Upaniṣad 1.18.48)
For them, saṃsāra consists of real entities characterized by being agents and enjoyers;
they transmigrate due to non-discrimination, based on ignorance regarding the appearance of a self.

If the intellect were to possess the appearance of consciousness and the Self were to have that as its very nature, then it would be logical for the Veda to instruct [the practitioner] regarding that [Self] using words such as "knowledge. (SamUpad I, 18.50)
Just as the meanings of the base and the suffix are seen in common worldly usage to be distinct yet sharing a single substratum, as in "he does" (karoti) or "he goes" (gacchati).
In the world, such dual dependence is not observed for these two [cognition and memory], nor is it so in the case of recollection;
what reason can be stated for their dual dependence regarding objects of knowledge? (Samupad I.18.52)

The appearance of a self expressed by the verbal suffix, and the meaning of the root which is the activity of cognition—both of these are falsely said to be "one knows" through non-discrimination. (Samupad I, 18.53)
There is no cognition on the part of the intellect, nor does activity exist for the self;
therefore, it is not logical to say that either of them "knows. (Samyukta Āgama Upadeśa I, 18.54)
Nor is it tenable to say that cognition is expressed by this term as a positive entity;
for the Self is not mere transformation, according to the teaching that "the Self is eternal. (SamUpad I.18.55)

The state of being expressible by the word "intellect" does not belong to the intellect itself, for there is no instrument without an agent; nor is it defined by verbal expressions denoting the object, such as "it is known. (Samupad I.18.56)
For those for whom the Self is not even one—always free from suffering and change—the Self would always be subject to verbal designation and knowability. (Samyukta Āgama 18.57)
When the agent of the "I"-notion is regarded as the Self, then the primary meaning of the word [ātman] is maintained;
however, because it possesses hunger and other such qualities, its status as the Self is not accepted in the Śruti.
Alas, in that case, there is no primary meaning nor any figurative one whatsoever for words such as "he knows"; nevertheless, an interpretation must still be provided. (Samupad I.18.59)
If words were not in accordance with reality, the Veda too would lack authority; and that is not desired. Therefore, its validity must be accepted based on established consensus.

If the consensus of the deluded world were to be accepted as the absence of self, then it would follow that the doctrine of the Materialists (Lokāyatika) is established, which is undesirable. (Samupad I, 18.61)
If it is argued that [the Veda] is established by the consensus of those who are diligent [in its study], then, as before, it is difficult to distinguish [it from error];
nor is this Veda a valid means of knowledge, for it lacks a basis of comprehension or even correspondence with reality.
For humans, the commonality of the mirror-face is indeed desired for the face;
for the reflection of the face is seen in the form of a face. (SamUpad I, 18.63)

In whatever [object] there is the manifestation of whichever [cognition], everyone in the world naturally says "he knows" that action due to the non-discrimination between those two alone. (SamUpad I.18.64)
By superimposing agency upon the intellect, it is said that "it knows," and thus it is called the knower;
likewise, by superimposing consciousness upon the intellect, its state of being a knower is spoken of here.
Since the knowledge that is the very nature of the self is eternal light according to the Vedic revelation,
it is therefore never produced by the intellect, nor by the self, nor by anything else.
Just as people in the world have the notion of "I" with respect to the body and speak of the body's agency in knowing,
so too [they attribute] the agency of cognition to the intellect and likewise to the self.

"But by means of these very Buddhist conditions, which are produced in such a way and resemble consciousness, people who are logicians, being deluded, say that knowledge is created. (Samupad I, 18.68)

Therefore, because of the non-discrimination between the light of cognition and the intellect, there arise the verbal expressions such as "he knows," the corresponding cognition, and the memory thereof. (Samyukta-pañjikā I, 18.69)
Just as the reflection cast upon a face conforms to the mirror,
so too is it held that the appearance of the knower conforms to the attributes of the intellect.
Therefore, the mental factors, illuminated by the reflection of the self within the intellect,
appear as if they were apprehenders, just as firebrands and the like appear to be burning.
"The apprehenders manifest themselves by themselves and are themselves [the objects]," thus do the followers of the Sugata negate the existence of an apprehender. (SamUpad I, 18.72)
If this is so, they are not visible to others; then let it be explained how that is prevented.
For if their existence and non-existence are always such that they cannot be grasped by another, [how can they be known]? 18.73.
The claim that there is a continuous cognizer of them is likewise [untenable], because the lack of consciousness remains equal even when another cognizer exists. (Samupad I, 18.74)

If it is thought that accomplishment occurs in the presence of a witness, [we reply] no; for the witness provides no assistance, and because this consequence would apply to other cases as well. (SamUpad I.18.75)

A listener who is both desirous [of liberation] and suffering may be either one who possesses direct perception or otherwise; yet, you do not accept that such a person possesses both suffering and the state of being desirous. (Samupad I,18.76)
One who is the agent and the supervisor does not deserve to grasp at "I am real";
the false statement "I am indeed real" is not even tenable according to the Śruti.
If the Śruti were to speak of both [the self and the body] without making a distinction, then one might accept it as such;
but our [position] is that it would speak of "you" alone, having clearly distinguished [the two]. (SamUpad I, 18.78)
If [the self] were to reside in the continuum of conditions (*pratyayānvayi*), the aforementioned fault would follow.
If you say that "you" resides in direct perception (*adhyakṣa*), then how could there be [a single self] in the two perceptions of "I"? (Samupad I, 18.79)
In this context, there must indeed be a relation that would allow one to designate [the self] as "you";
for if it were the relation of seer and seen, how could it apply to the inactive witness? (Samupad I, 18.80)

Even if there were identity with the perception despite its being non-productive, the cognition "I have the perception of the self" would not occur if the relationship [between them] were not apprehended. (Samupad I, 18.81)

If you think that the apprehension of the relationship [between word and meaning] comes from scripture (*śāstra*), it is not so; for the threefold defects previously mentioned would apply, or else there would be the thought, "It is my [apprehension]. (Samupad I, 18.82)
When the intellect always shines as the form of the Seer (the Self), even its cognitive modifications become like sparks from heated iron. (Samupad I.18.83)
Appearance and its absence belong to the limit of perception and not otherwise;
for the world, these two would exist through logical reasoning, and their apprehension would likewise be so.
"Surely, in this way, there would be a transference of the seer, like fire into an iron ball;
but that has been refuted by the example of the reflection of a face in a mirror. (Samudaya-pada 1.85)
"The black [iron] has the appearance of red"—this is what is called "seen" (dṛṣṭa).
There is a similarity between the seen and the example, but not in every respect anywhere. (Samupad I, 18.86)
In the same way, the mind, though appearing as consciousness, would be like consciousness;
just as the reflection of a face in a mirror is a mere appearance, and such an appearance is declared to be false. (Samādhirāja Sūtra 18.87)
The claim that "mind is volition" is devoid of both scripture and logic; for by that same reasoning, it would follow that the body, as well as the eyes and other sense organs, are also mind.
If it is argued, "Let that [self] also exist," we say no, because that would entail the position of the Lokāyatikas.
Furthermore, there is no cognition such as "I am the seer" if there is no appearance [of a self] in the mind. (Samupad I.18.89)

If the cognition "I am" were absent, the statement "That thou art" would be meaningless; this teaching becomes purposeful only for one who knows the distinction between the "thou" (the empirical self) and the "I" (the true Self).
The notions "this is mine" and "I am this" should be understood as belonging to the *yuṣmad* [the "you"] alone; there is no doubt about this.
The notion "I" is intended for the *asmad* [the "we"], and the notion "this is I" belongs to both. (Samupad I, 18.91)
Their status as primary or subordinate is held to be relative to one another;
likewise, the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified should be understood through reasoning. (Samādhipradīpa 18.92)
Both of these [terms] are qualifiers of the "middle" one; just as one says "the wealthy man" or "the owner of cows," so too [is it said] "the body of the I-maker. (Samupad I, 18.93)
Everything is always mounted upon the intellect, along with the ego-maker (ahaṃkartṛ), for the witness;
therefore, the Knower, never touching anything at all, is the illuminator of everything.
All this that has been stated according to worldly understanding is contrary [to reality];
for those of undiscriminating intellect everything exists, but for the discriminating, nothing exists at all.
For positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) pertain to both the word-meaning and the word;
this very logic applies here in determining the meaning of the expression "I. 18.96.
"In this state of deep sleep, [the statement] 'I did not see anything else even slightly' does not negate one's own vision, but rather negates the cognitive content. (Samupad I.18.97)

"The Self-luminous is indeed not [an object] for the seer"— thus the scripture itself has declared the existence of consciousness, its immutability, and likewise the disappearance of that cognition, distinguishing between the cognition and the awareness thereof. (SamUpad I, 18.98)

When the meaning of the sentence has been thus understood through the authority of the scripture and worldly convention, the Śruti declares, "That thou art," in order to remove the delusion of the listener. (Samupad I, 18.99)
Just as Brahmā dispelled the darkness of the son of Daśaratha by his word alone,
he did not mention any further effort for the sake of awakening him to his own nature as Viṣṇu.
That which is the ultimate ground of the word "I" within the inner self, the light—that very thing is expressed by the words "Thou art That"; the fruit therein is liberation.
If that [self] were not to exist merely upon hearing [of it], then its existence would certainly have to be established through its effects;
yet, even prior to such worldly activity, the existence of the self is accepted by itself.
For the sake of liberation from hunger and other such states, valid knowledge arises at that very time;
regarding the meaning of statements such as "That thou art," there is no doubt across the three periods of time.
Because it is free from any obstruction and because it is itself of the nature of direct experience, valid cognition must indeed arise therein within its own self; of this there is no doubt.
Does one think "I am indeed Being," or does one apprehend something else?
If it is Being itself, then let the word "I" be accepted as having its primary meaning in Being. (Samyukta Upaniṣad I, 18.105)
If it were something else, then the apprehension of a self would be entirely false;
therefore, since there is no understanding of an exclusion here, there can be no grasping of a primary [self]. (SamUpad I, 18.106)
When the subject and the object appear as such, that constitutes their nature as object;
and because those two are devoid of consciousness, the fruit is attributed to consciousness. (Samupad I.18.107)
Even though [the Self] is immutable (*kūṭastha*), it is the fit locus for the fruit, just as victory and the like belong to the king;
this is because of the two reasons [previously stated]: its non-selfhood and [the fact that it is not the agent] of the action and the cognition. (Samupad I, 18.108)
Just as the reflection appearing in a mirror is of the very form of the face, so too, that which appears in the mirror of cognition is indeed the "I. (Samudrapala’s Upadeśa 18.109)
Thus, there would be the realization "I am existent" and not otherwise;
even the instruction "That thou art" would be purposeless due to the absence of such a gateway.
If there were instruction for a listener, it would thus possess purposefulness;
if being a listener is not admitted for the supervisor, to whom would that [instruction] belong? (SamUpad I, 18.111)
If it is thought that [the assistance] comes from the intellect alone in the presence of the supervisor, we reply:
no, for there is no benefit produced by that [supervisor], just as none is imagined [to come] from a piece of wood.
If [it is argued that] something produced by that [mind] exists within the intellect (*buddhi*), then surely it has been transformed [into an object].
And what fault is there even in the case of a mental appearance (*ābhāsa*), provided it is supported by scripture and other means of valid cognition?

If it is argued that there is transformation within the appearance, it is not so; for it is like the appearance of a rope and the like, as well as a snake and the like, and as I have stated, like the appearance of a face in a mirror. (Samyukta-upadeśa I, 18.114)
If it is argued that the appearance as a self is not established because it is distinct from the apprehension of a self,
whereas the face and so forth are established as distinct [from their reflections], then here there is a mutual dependence.
If the perceiver were established as separate [from the appearance], then the appearance would belong to him;
but if the appearance belongs to him, it must indeed be distinct from the perceiver. (Samupad I, 18.116)
It is not so in a dream, because the cognition and the seeing are not established as separate;
since the chariot and so forth are absent there, the cognition is apprehended by itself.
For a cognition, permeated by comprehension, arises in the form of its object;
whatever form it takes, that is considered the external object. (Samupad I, 18.118)
Because it is the most desired object of action, that [agent] is employed toward the effect;
and that upon which the form is imposed is here called the instrument (*karaṇa*). (SamUpad I, 18.119)
When one is pervaded by whatever appearance, that is called "the known.
He who discerns these three here is a knower of the Self. (Samyutta-Upaniṣad I, 18.120)
Cognitions that are correctly apprehended, doubtful, or falsely stated are variable;
there is only one realization among them, while the distinction is imposed by the cognitions themselves.
Just as the diversity of a gem is understood through its various facets, so too impurity and transformation are entirely dependent upon conditions. (Samyukta Āgama 18.122)
In this context, the expansion, the grasping, and the accomplishment of the cognitive determinations (pratyayas) arise from another source;
because they are not directly perceived, that very process is said to be like inference, resembling a lamp.
How could anyone cause an ignorant person to understand by means of some valid cognition?
Rather, it is only through the exclusion of the other [possibilities] that the remainder is understood even without a valid cognition.
If it is argued that cessation is expressed here by verbal testimony alone, then because direct perception is not established, the consequence is nothing but emptiness.
If it is asked, "How can you be conscious while being the body?", [we reply] no, because it is not established;
for only when the distinctness of the conscious [self] is established would this [objection] hold, since otherwise there would be the abandonment of what is other.
The witness-consciousness itself exists as an immediate perception for the conscious being;
thus, the awakening would be exactly the same for the ignorant one as it is for the proponent of non-existence.
"Based on the worldly convention that 'I knew this,' the instrument, the object, and the agent are indeed established here as existing within a single moment. (Samudrapariśuddhi 18.128)
Even though memory is a valid means of knowledge, simultaneity is perceived due to its rapidity;
first there is apprehension by the senses, and subsequently memory occurs in exactly the same sequence.
The cognition "I know this" and the cognition "me" certainly arise with mutual dependence;
wherever a distinction is required, there can never be simultaneity.

Furthermore, since the three factors are present here even when the self is the object of perception, the agency attached to the self would not belong to the instrument or the object. (Samupad I.18.131)
That which is intended by the agent to be pervaded by his action is known as the object (karman);
for this reason, its dependence on the agent is intended, not dependence on anything else. (Samupad I, 18.132)
The establishment of all categories of objects must proceed from verbal testimony, or from inference, or from some other means of valid cognition; it cannot be otherwise for one who is ignorant.
The existence of a supervisor would have to be established either by a means of valid cognition or even without one;
however, its establishment without [a means of cognition] is of no use to one who is ignorant.
If it is held that ignorance belongs to that very [self], then when there is knowledge, there would have to be another means of cognition;
and if ignorance belonged to someone else, then upon the cognition of that [object], ignorance would certainly persist [in the self].
Establishment (siddhi) may consist in the cognition of [an object], or in its own attainment, or indeed something else entirely;
regarding the case of cognition, you should recall the two positions just mentioned. (Samupad I, 18.136)
If accomplishment were the attainment of its own self, then effort toward it would be useless,
since a thing is already established by its own causes and is well-known to the entire world.
Therefore, in the discourse concerning knowledge and the object of knowledge, "establishment" is said to be "the state of being known";
the establishment of the knower and the object of knowledge consists in their being known, not in their mere acquisition of self-existence.

If clarity and establishedness are postulated for the object, the agent, and so forth, then clarity and lack of clarity would belong to something other [than consciousness], and not to the self. (Samupad I, 18.139)

But for one who is not a seer and is blind, there is no manifestation of a jar at all; if it is claimed that the manifestation of the agent and so forth is desired [to occur], then that manifestation must have a seer as its instrumental agent. (Samupad I, 18.140)
Tell me, what would there be within that experience by virtue of your dependence upon it?
If the experiencer were desired [as distinct], for us he too is nothing but experience itself.

"For although the nature of cognition is undivided, it appears as if possessed of a distinction between the grasped object, the grasping subject, and self-awareness, to those whose vision is distorted."

[That which is their coming-into-being is itself the action, and that very thing is called the agent. If its existence is its perishability, then let its agency be accepted in the same way. If you say that no property whatsoever is intended, then there is the fallacy of abandoning your own thesis. (Samuccaya-pañjikā I, 18.143)
Surely, properties such as existence are the negations of non-existence and so forth;
therefore, perishability does not belong to the primary elements, for those [properties] are their specific characteristics.
Destruction is limited to its own specific characteristic; destruction is the cessation of non-destruction.
For a non-cow, "cowness" is its non-existence, but that is not the specific characteristic of a cow.
Even that object which is expressed by the word "moment" (kṣaṇa) is, for you, simply the absence of others;
although there is no difference in the nature of non-existence, it is nevertheless distinguished by various names.
How could there be multiplicity for a single entity according to you through different names?
If [apoha] is the exclusion of different things, how can it reside in a cow?
None of the absences, nor any particulars,
nor names, universals, and so forth, can ever differentiate consciousness, because they are themselves devoid of differentiation.
If you desire perception or inference for the sake of worldly transaction, it must certainly be accepted as involving the distinctions between actions and their factors (kārakas). 18.149.
Therefore, whether it be blue, yellow, or a jar and so forth as a qualifier,
that must be admitted to exist within consciousness, by which it is experienced.

Just as form and the other [objects] might be distinct from their perceiver because they are the perceived, so too the cognition would be distinct from its object because it is the manifestor, like a lamp. (Samudaya-pada 18.151)
What kind of relationship could possibly exist between the witness-consciousness (*adhyakṣa*) and the seeing (*dṛś*), apart from that which consists of the seer and the seen? (Samupad I.18.152)

Alternatively, the vision produced by the supervisor might pervade the object of perception; or perhaps some benefit for the cognitions might be produced by the eternal supervisor. (Samupad I, 18.153)
And that resemblance to it (the object) has been stated previously, as well as its pervasion over jars and other things;
for just as light and so forth pervade objects, so too does the intellect, because it is a manifestor.

Just as a jar situated in light becomes mounted upon the intellect, so too there would be a pervasion by the intellect; the mounting of the jar would occur when the intellect has pervaded it, and thus there would be a sequence in that pervasion.
First there would be the pervasion of conditions, and from that, the favoring of the self;
such a sequence is untenable for an all-pervading witness, just as in the case of time, space, and so forth.
That whose apprehension of objects occurs in dependence upon causes, and while a remainder of the graspable still exists, is subject to transformation, like the mind. (Samupad I, 18.157)
The cognition "I am the perceiver" is indeed the determination of the intellect (buddhi);
it does not belong to the perceiver itself, because the perceiver is devoid of distinctions, and for that reason, there is nothing further beyond it.
If liberation were experienced by the agent as "I [am liberated]," then freedom from pleasure and pain would not be possible for one who possesses the sense of "I. (Samupad I, 18.159)

The conviction that "I am suffering," which certainly arises from the conceit regarding the body and so forth, is like the perception of a [golden] earring for one who identifies with the inner self. (Samupad I, 18.160)
In this world, one who lacks discernment is subverted by a condition through discernment;
in the opposite case, there would be non-existence at the end due to the invalidity of the means of knowledge.
Suffering arises from burning, cutting, or destruction, and not otherwise for the Self;
for indeed, when one person undergoes burning or the like, another never becomes suffering.
Because I am intangible and bodiless, I can never be burned;
therefore, [this grief] arises from false identification, like the death [one feels] when a son dies. (Samupad I, 18.163)
For the notion "I am the coil" is indeed sublated by the discriminating person;
likewise, the cognition "I am miserable" is always sublated by the pure sense of "I."
When suffering is established, that capacity for it would belong to the eternal Self;
one becomes miserable through false identification, and thus there is no destruction of the purpose [of the Self]. (Samupad I, 18.165)
Just as one who is untouched perceives touch, and one who is immovable perceives motion and so forth,
so too does one perceive mental suffering as belonging to oneself due to a lack of discrimination.
Suffering is dispelled by the intellect of discernment, just as movement [is stopped] by effort;
the mind proceeds toward non-discernment even against its will due to its own inherent nature. (Samyukta Āgama 18.167)
Then suffering is perceived; it does not exist for one who is in a state of immobility.
Therefore, that suffering is not at all possible within the inner Self (pratyagātman).
Because the word *tvam* and [the word *asau*] share the same locus, this [substitution] would occur like [the substitution of] *nīla-aśva*;
for the word *tvam* has that [other person] as its referent due to its connection with a term expressing the absence of suffering (*nirduḥkha*). (SamUpad I, 18.169)
Likewise, because the word "that" denotes the inner self (pratyagātman), the sentence "You are the tenth" would apply to the inner self. (SamUpad I, 18.170)

For, without abandoning one's own [limited] purpose, these two [means of knowledge] convey a superior object; they culminate in the realization of the inner Self. Therefore, no other object can be contrary to this [ultimate] object.
For, just as one who does not see oneself as the completer of ten due to the loss of the ninth cognition would desire to know one's own self, so it is with people. (Samyukta Āgama-pada I, 18.172)
Because his eyes are bound by ignorance, his intellect is perpetually carried away by desires;
thus he does not perceive the Self, the pure Seer, just as one fails to see the tenth person.
"Thou art the Tenth"—through such statements as "That thou art," one realizes one's own Self as the witness within the entire internal organ. (Samupad I, 18.174)

"There must be this word first and that word later in a sentence"—such a rule does not exist at all in the Veda; rather, the coherence of words is established through their meaning. (SamUpad I.18.175)
For there is a recollection of the meanings of the words heard in a sentence;
through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the understanding of the sentence-meaning arises from that. (SamUpad I.18.176)

When the meaning of the words in eternal sentences is analyzed for the purpose of transmitting the knowledge of the sentence-meaning, then a question [regarding that analysis] is not appropriate. (Samupad I, 18.177)
The statement of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), however, serves for the recollection of word-meanings;
for without such recollection, the meaning of the sentence cannot be understood by anyone. (Samupad I, 18.178)

Because the meaning of the word *tvaṃ* (you) is not clearly distinguished within sentences such as "That thou art," the sentence-meaning—namely, "I am eternally liberated"—is not revealed at all. (SamUpad I, 18.179)
The statement of positive and negative concomitance serves for the sake of distinguishing that [meaning], and not otherwise;
for when the referent of the term *tvam* is distinguished, it is like a bilva fruit placed in the palm of one's hand. (SamUpad I, 18.180)

In this way, the meaning of the sentence is manifested solely from the referent of the word "I," through the determination of the inner self by means of the negation of the notion "one who suffers. (SamUpad I, 18.181)
In that case, when such a meaning is possible, it is not proper for those skilled in the meaning of words and sentences to abandon what is heard and conceive of an unheard meaning. (Samupad I.18.182)

Just as the cooking of *kṛṣṇala* seeds and the like would subvert perception and other means of knowledge, how could these [scriptural statements], which resemble perceptions and so forth, subvert the Vedic word? 18.183.
When the cognition "I am suffering" exists, the cognition "I am free from suffering" does not arise;
for even if it resembles perception and other means of knowledge, it is not produced by verbal testimony due to its lack of non-erroneousness.

"If, when one has been suffering in a dream due to causes such as burning or cutting, that suffering were not sublated by statements occurring at that very time, [then the waking experience would likewise be real]. (Samupad I, 18.185)
In that case, let the cessation of suffering be desired even before [the attainment of liberation];
for nowhere is a continuum of suffering or of delusion ever observed.

If one knows that the inner self possesses the nature of the Self through the sublation of the notion "I am miserable"—just as one realizes the tenth person by means of the ninth—then there is no contradiction. (Samupad I, 18.187)
The realization of eternal liberation arises from the sentence and not from anything else;
furthermore, the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence is preceded by the recollection of the meanings of its constituent words. (Samupad I, 18.188)
Through positive and negative concomitance, the meaning of a word is certainly remembered;
in this way, one realizes the Self as being free from suffering and devoid of action.

From such statements as "Being alone [this was in the beginning]," a clearer cognition arises regarding the inner self, just as it does from the statement "You are the tenth. (Samkṣepa-Śārīraka I.18.190)
Just as all suffering in a dream ceases through awakening,
so too does the state of suffering belonging to the Self at all times cease through the knowledge of the inner Self.
In the case of the *kṛṣṇala* weight and so forth, the production of valid cognition occurs because the object is other than that [intended] and lacks softness;
however, this is not the case with sentences such as "That thou art," because there is no contradiction.
In this sentence "That thou art," the two terms "that" and "art" have their meanings already known;
yet, without the assistance of the recollection of the meaning of "thou," the sentence would not produce valid knowledge. (Samupad I, 18.193)
In the sense of having a common locus, the word "thou" (asi) would be [the predicate] for the word "that" (tat);
the word "that" has the meaning of the inner self (pratyagātman), and "thou" likewise has the meaning of that word. 1.18.194.
Both [suffering and the inner self] would exclude each other's nature as suffering and as the inner self;
and thus they would mutually convey the meaning of "not this, not this."
Thus, when the fruit of the statement "That thou art" is being understood, how can its lack of authority be asserted by claiming that it depends upon ritual action? 18.196.
Therefore, the injunction "one should perform [the rite]" at the beginning, middle, and end is contradictory;
hence, it should not be postulated because it is not heard in the scripture, and the abandonment of what is heard would also be purposeless.

Just as satisfaction is experienced [from eating], yet it is not understood from the sentence; so too is the transformation of cow dung into milk-porridge the sustaining power of the sentence. (Samupad I, 18.198)

It is true that in this way, through the sentence, there is an understanding of transcendence regarding what is not the Self; however, it is not so with respect to the inner Self, for [that realization] is as certain as the attainment of a number. 18.199 (SamUpad I)
Let it be accepted that [the self] has its own means of valid cognition, as "self-cognizability" is a synonym for this;
for when the notion of "I" has ceased, our own experience of the self is established. (Samupad I, 18.200)
Suffering is the object of the intellects; he for whom those [intellects] are considered objects—how could there be any connection with suffering for him, the inner self who is pure consciousness?
The act of seeing itself would be experienced by its own nature as experience;
the arising of this cognition in the form of that [object] is known as "experience. (Samupad I, 18.202)
"You alone are that perfected one, liberation itself, free from hunger and other such needs;
how then can it be said that you are subject to hearing and so forth? This is a contradiction. (Samupad I, 18.203)
If it were thought that "it will be established," then hearing and the other [means] would be required;
in that case, liberation would be non-eternal, and otherwise, the statement would be contradictory. (Samupad I, 18.204)

If a distinction between the hearer and the object to be heard were intended, this [consequence] would follow; thus there would be a contradiction of the intended meaning, and the statement would not be tenable in any way. (SamUpad I.18.205)
If one who desires to act should think, "I am liberated," having thus known the Self, that person is a fool, even if he opens up the scriptures. (Samupad I, 18.206)
For that which is already established has nothing further to be done, and that which possesses an effect is not yet established;
by attempting to rely upon both simultaneously, one deceives oneself. (Samudrapāla Upadeśa 18.207)
The mere fact that "liberation is accomplished for you" is demonstrated so that the listener may understand its reality and inquire, "How might this be? (Samupad I, 18.208).

"It is experienced through direct perception that 'I am the agent' and 'I am suffering'; from that [perception], there arises the effort [in the form]: 'May I not be the agent and the sufferer. (Samupad I,18.209)

The Śruti declares that reasoning and other means must be employed for the sake of realizing that [Self], in order to bring about the experience of its established nature through the restatement of agency and other attributes. (Samupad I, 18.210)
Having grasped even such contradictory meanings as "I am free from suffering, inactive, desireless, perfected, and liberated," how indeed could he maintain them? (Samupad I, 18.211)
"How is it that my experience is that one who possesses desire and performs action remains unaccomplished?
Therefore, you ought to explain that to me, for I am the opposite [of what I expect]. (Samyukta-upaniṣad 18.212)
The question is relevant only in this context, not for the sake of experiencing liberation;
that which is contradicted by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is the subject that deserves inquiry here.
The notion "I am liberated" or "I am existent" arises from another form of conceit;
because it is produced by a semblance of direct perception, it deserves the inquiry into suffering.
That which was asked and desired—the state of being free from suffering—is what I seek:
"How indeed might this suffering of mine cease in every respect? (Samyukta Āgama, 18.215)
Thus, that which is to be spoken in accordance with the question— which brings about the cessation of suffering—
is not subject to doubt regarding its validity within the Veda once its authority is established.
Therefore, that statement conveys the state of being liberated from the self;
however, it should be spoken in such a way that its meaning is consistent with reality, provided there is no contradiction with anything else.
No other experience of the self is possible apart from this, according to the Vedic revelation: "The knower of the known is itself unknown to those who know. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.17)

For the sake of discriminating the meaning of the word "thou," the renunciation of all actions indeed becomes a means, in accordance with the injunctions such as "being tranquil" and "being self-controlled. (SamUpad I, 18.219)
One should perceive the meaning of "Thou" as the inner self, the Self within oneself;
thereafter, one perceives the meaning of the Great Sentence as the Self alone, which is everything. (Samnyāsa Upaniṣad 1.18.220)

When the meaning of the sentence "all is the Self" has been cognized through this means of valid knowledge, how could an injunction apply to that [Self], given that no other means of knowledge can establish its non-existence? (Samupad I, 18.221)
Therefore, after the realization of the meaning of the sentence, there can be no further injunction to perform ritual action;
for the two cognitions "I am Brahman" and "I am an agent" are contradictory.

For this knowledge—"I am Brahman"—is not sublated by the notion "I am an agent," nor by the idea "I am one with desires and bound," which arises from fallacious means of knowledge. (Samupad I, 18.223)

When, through the scripture, the firm conviction arises that "I am Brahman, I am not another," then that intellect is [liberated], just as the intellect identifying the body as the self [is sublated]. (SamUpad I, 18.224)
He who has attained freedom from fear after being in fear and strives for that purpose, would not, if he were independent, wish to go back to a state of fear. (Samyukta-upaniṣad I, 18.225)

How could there be the attainment of acting according to one's own whims for one who, having awakened through the ignorance of the meanings of words, seeks the experience of the meaning of the sentence through the injunctions for renunciation and so forth? (Samupad I, 18.226)
Therefore, all this which was previously stated by us is established.
For one who is detached from something does not engage with it;
since the seeker of liberation is detached from the three worlds, why would he strive for anything here? (Samupad I, 18.228)

Even when tormented by hunger, one does not wish to eat poison; knowing that his thirst has been quenched by sweet food, a wise man, being no fool, does not desire to devour it. (Samyukta-upadeśa 18.229)
Salutations to that true Guru who, like a bee, extracted for us the finest honey of the nectar of knowledge from the flowers of the Vedānta scriptures. (Samupad I, 18.230)
Thus ends the section on "That Thou Art. (Samyuktopaniṣad I, 18)
Having applied the medical treatment consisting of the medicine of knowledge and dispassion, which causes the destruction of the fever of craving,
one does not undergo the suffering born from the complication of the fever of desire— the misery of being joined with hundreds of bodily afflictions.
"You strive for the misfortune [of others] through the notions of 'I' and 'mine,' while others desire your success.
You have no understanding of their welfare, nor do I have any desire for yours; therefore, tranquility alone is appropriate for your mind. (Samyukta Āgama 19.2)
Since there is nothing other than the supreme, eternal [Self], I am forever satisfied; therefore, I have no desire for anything.
I am eternally liberated and do not seek welfare; therefore, O mind, strive even more toward your own tranquility. (Samyukta Upaniṣad 19.3)
He who has indeed transcended the garland of the six waves is the very Self of the universe according to our scripture;
furthermore, this is established by me through valid means of knowledge. Therefore, your mental effort regarding this is entirely in vain.
When you are at peace, that notion of duality does not exist, from which the world falls into delusion through illusion (māyā).
For grasping is the cause of what arises from illusion; when one is liberated from grasping, that [illusion] no longer exists for anyone.
I have no delusion caused by your actions, for you have awakened to reality and are indeed unattached and immutable.
There is no distinction between a prior and a subsequent reality for us; therefore, your mental exertion is truly in vain.

Since I am eternal, I am therefore not otherwise; for if there were connection with modification, there would be impermanence. I am always luminous, and therefore non-dual; thus it is established that the conceptualized is non-existent. (Samādhirāja Sūtra Upadeśa I, 19.7)
O mind, you are of the nature of non-existence here; for when examined through reasoning, your existence is not tenable.
Since that which exists does not perish and that which does not exist is never born, both [existence and non-existence] are therefore held to be non-existent for you.
The seer, the seen, and likewise the seeing—all that is indeed your own mental construction, for it is a delusion.
Indeed, an object of sight is never perceived as distinct from the act of seeing; thus, it is not divided in sleep nor is it divided in waking.
Conceptualization likewise becomes non-dual because it lacks any objective reality, like a circle of fire produced by a whirling torch;
since there is no difference in their causal capacity, and since selves do not exist [as separate entities], their non-duality is determined from scripture. // SamUpad_I,19.10 //
If those conscious entities were mutually distinct, then because they possess finite dimensions, their destruction would be certain;
for the destruction of all things that are divided is observed, and thus there would be the total liberation of the entire world.
I have no one, nor do I belong to anyone, since I am non-dual; for indeed, nothing imagined exists.
I am unimagined, established from the beginning; it is only through conceptualization that duality is imagined. (Samādhirāja Sūtra 19.12)
Furthermore, conceptual construction does not exist in the absence [of an object]; thus, because there is something else that exists, non-existence does not follow.
For the conceptual construction of yours has also proceeded from what was previously established, and that was not [previously] conceptualized.
For both of those which are perceived by you are non-existent; yet, simply because something is not seen does not mean it has no existence at all.
Since the conceptualization of "existent" and "non-existent" proceeds from that [perception], and because it is like an investigation, so too is the non-dual reality existent.

If that which you have postulated as existent is accepted by you for the sake of investigation, yet it is non-existent [upon such investigation], then it remains exactly as it was before the investigation ceased; if that is not desired, then it is all the more accepted as truly existent.
If it is argued that what is non-existent is indeed the same as the existent, that is not so, because it would be devoid of purpose, being equivalent to the horn of a donkey.
For in the case of the non-existent, there is no cause for purposefulness; therefore, it is not otherwise in the case of the opposite. (Samupad I, 19.16)
Furthermore, because it is unestablished and because it is the cause of investigation, the duality has indeed issued forth through illusion;
for this is established by scripture, tradition, and reasoning, and it is not tenable otherwise.
Moreover, because it is distinct from conceptual construction (*vikalpana*) and because it was established prior to hearing [the teachings], the non-dual reality is free from conceptualization;
thus, by means of the negations "not this, not this," even that which has been conceptually constructed is here negated for the sake of establishing the remainder. (Samādhirāja-sūtra 19.18)
Even though the unborn, non-dual, and imperishable is thus unimagined, those who conceptualize it as being or non-being through successive births,
enter continuously into existence, old age, and death, which arise from the illusion of their own minds.
If there is no becoming or ceasing to be, there is no persistence; nor is there anything other than that, so birth cannot occur otherwise.
Since what exists does not become non-existent and what does not exist does not come into existence, there is neither action nor an agent; therefore, for this reason also, it is unborn.
If that which does not perform the desired action were not a causal agent, then surely nothing else would be a non-agent;
for there is no distinction between the existent and the non-existent once existence has ceased, just as there is no certainty regarding the two ends of a scale.
If that reversal of existence and non-existence is not accepted, how could there be becoming when existence and non-existence are established?
Since these two are established as distinct, there is no birth; for indeed, [this] mind belongs to no one.
Moreover, even granting that existence is accepted as you desire, I say that there is no purpose for me in your exertion;
for there can be neither decrease nor increase, since what is non-existent by itself cannot come into being from another, nor can those two [decrease and increase] possess existence.
For the permanent and the impermanent are not joined with one another, nor is an effect logically applicable to them;
therefore, nothing whatsoever is desired for anything at all, since reality itself is beyond the scope of verbal definition.

Therefore, the wise person, having constantly observed through reasoning and scripture that which is equal, ever-shining, and liberated from the dualistic conceptualization of existence and non-existence, attains complete Nirvana like a lamp. (Samādhirāja Sūtra 19.25)
That which is unknowable to those who know nothing else, yet is easily known by bad logicians in another way—
having perceived it thus, one who grasps no qualities does not fall into delusion regarding the qualityless, due to being freed from the defect of grasping.
Therefore, the destruction of grasping is not desired in any other way; for grasping itself is the cause of the deluded intellect.
Indeed, when grasping is without cause—just as fire without fuel—it shall proceed to supreme peace. (Samādhirāja Sūtra I.19.27)

Salutations to those gurus by whom this supreme knowledge was formerly beheld—this nectar of wisdom churned from the ocean of the Vedas, just as the great-souled gods extracted [the nectar] from the great sea. *Samayopaniṣad* I.19.28.
Thus ends the section on the destruction of fever. (Samhitopaniṣad I, 19)
Now, we shall explain the method of instruction for the means to liberation, for the sake of those who desire liberation, who possess faith, and who seek it.

This knowledge, which is the means for attaining liberation, is to be imparted to a disciple who has become dispassionate toward everything impermanent that is achievable through worldly means; who has renounced the desire for son, wealth, and worlds; who has entered the supreme state of the wandering mendicant (paramahaṃsa-pārivrājya); who is endowed with tranquility, self-control, compassion, and other virtues; who possesses the qualities of a disciple well-known in the scriptures; who is pure; who has approached according to the prescribed rule; and who has been tested by birth, conduct, behavior, learning, and lineage.
He should repeat it again and again until its mastery becomes firm.
And scripture says: "Having examined... the knowledge of Brahman in its true essence.
For knowledge firmly grasped leads to the highest good and to the continuity of the self;
and the continuity of knowledge serves to favor living beings, like a boat for one desiring to cross a river.
And the Śāstra says: "Even if one were to give him this earth, surrounded by water and filled with wealth, this alone would be more than that.
Otherwise, there would be no attainment of knowledge, for it is said: "The man who has a teacher knows," and "From the teacher alone is knowledge known [and reaches its most perfect state]."
“‘The teacher is the one who makes one cross over; his right knowledge is said here to be the raft,’” according to such scriptural passages and traditional texts (smṛti). // SamUpad_II,1.3 //

Having ascertained through signs that the disciple has not grasped the knowledge, [the teacher] should remove the causes of that non-grasping—namely, demerit (*adharma*), worldly negligence (*laukikapramāda*), lack of discrimination regarding eternal and non-eternal things (*nityānityavastuviveka*), lack of firmness in prior learning, preoccupation with worldly thoughts, and pride regarding one's caste and so forth—by means of their opposites: the restraints (*yama*) such as freedom from anger and non-violence, and the observances (*niyama*) prescribed by *śruti* and *smṛti* which are not inconsistent with knowledge. SamUpad_II,1.4 //
And one should cause [the disciple] to correctly grasp the qualities such as humility (amānitva) and others, which are the means to knowledge.
And the teacher—endowed with the capacity for reasoning and refutation, for grasping and retaining [knowledge], and with tranquility, self-control, compassion, grace, and so forth;

one who has mastered the traditional scriptures, is unattached to seen and unseen enjoyments, has abandoned all means of worldly action, is a knower of Brahman, established in Brahman, of unbroken conduct, free from defects such as hypocrisy, pride, deceit, guile, illusion, envy, falsehood, egoism, and the sense of "mine-ness," and whose sole purpose is the welfare of others, seeking only the application of knowledge—should first instruct [the student]: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone."
"In the beginning, there was only the One, without a second," "where one sees nothing else," and "all this is indeed the Self."

“Brahman alone is all this,” “In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone,” and “All this is indeed Brahman”— such are the scriptural passages (śruti) whose purpose is to establish the oneness of the Self. (SamUpad II.1.6)

And having taught it, one should cause [the student] to grasp the definition of Brahman: "That Self which is free from evil," "That Brahman which is immediate and direct," and "That which is beyond hunger and thirst."
“Not this, not this”;
“neither gross nor subtle”;
“this one is ‘not this, not this’.”
“The unseen seer,” “consciousness-bliss,” “truth, knowledge, infinite.”
“In the invisible, the bodiless,” “This very one indeed,” “For it is without breath and without mind.”
“Indeed, he is unborn, both within and without”;
“He is a mass of consciousness alone”;
“Without interior or exterior.”
“‘That is indeed other than the known, and also other than the unknown,’ ‘Space, indeed, is the name,’ and so forth—by such scriptural passages. (SamUpad II.1.7)
And by the Smṛtis: "It is neither born nor does it die," "It takes upon itself the sin of no one," and "As space is eternally situated."
“Know me also as the Knower of the Field,” “It is said to be neither existent nor non-existent,” and “Because of being beginningless and devoid of qualities.”

“Having grasped the definition of the Supreme Self through such Śrutis and Smṛtis—such as ‘equal toward all beings’ and ‘the Supreme Person’—which are not contradicted by the characteristics declared in the Śruti, which aim at establishing the non-transmigratory nature of the Supreme Self, and which aim at establishing His non-difference from everything, [the teacher] should question the disciple—who desires to cross over the ocean of transmigratory existence—saying: ‘Who are you, O Somya? (SamUpad II.1.9)

If he should say: "I was the son of a Brāhmaṇa, of such-and-such a lineage, a religious student; now I am a householder, and now I am a wandering mendicant of the supreme order (paramahaṃsaparivrāṭ), desiring to cross over the ocean of saṃsāra with its great crocodiles of birth and death. (SamUpad II.1.10)
The teacher should say: "My dear boy, as soon as you die right here, your body will be eaten by birds or reduced to the state of earth;
how then do you wish to cross over the ocean of saṃsāra? For one who has been turned to ashes on this side of a river cannot cross to the other side of that river. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad II.1.11)
If he should say: "I am other than the body;
the body, however, is born and dies, it is consumed by old age, and it reaches the state of earth."
It is destroyed by weapons, fire, and the like, and it is afflicted by diseases and other such ailments.

Into this [body], I have entered again and again—like a bird entering its nest—under the power of my own performed merit and demerit; thus, upon the destruction of the body, I shall go to another body under the influence of merit and demerit.

Just as a bird, upon the destruction of its former nest, seeks another nest, even so have I, throughout beginningless saṃsāra, in the states of gods, animals, humans, and denizens of hell, abandoned each body acquired through the power of my own karma and taken up another, ever new.

"Being whirled about by my own karma like a water-wheel in the cycle of the continuous succession of birth and death, I have finally attained this body; now, weary of this wandering in the wheel of saṃsāra, I have approached the Blessed One for the sake of pacifying that wandering in the wheel of saṃsāra.
Therefore, I am indeed eternal and distinct from the body."
Bodies come and go for a person, just like garments. // SamUpad_II,1.12 //
The teacher should say: "Well spoken; you see correctly.
How could one who is a son of a Brahmin, of noble lineage, and a student (*brahmacārin*), or a householder, be a speaker of falsehood?"
"Now I am a wandering mendicant who is a supreme swan (paramahaṃsa-parivrāj)."
If he should say, "Venerable sir, how did I speak falsely? [Samyukta Āgama II.1.14]

To him the teacher should say: "Since you have identified with the body—which possesses distinctions of caste, lineage, and sacraments—as being the Self which is devoid of caste, lineage, and sacraments, by means of such statements as 'I am the son of a Brāhmaṇa' and 'I belong to such-and-such a lineage.'"
If he should ask: "How is it that the body possesses the impressions of caste and lineage, while I am devoid of the impressions of caste and lineage? // SamUpad_II,1.16 //

The teacher should say: "Listen, my dear, to how this body is distinct from you, possessing a different birth, lineage, and refinement, whereas you are devoid of birth, lineage, and refinement. Having said this, he should cause him to remember:

"You ought to remember, my dear, the Supreme Self, the Self of all, whose characteristics have been declared by such scriptural passages as 'In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone' (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1), and by the Smṛtis as well."
And its characteristic is defined by the Śrutis and the Smṛtis.

To bring about the recollection of the characteristic of the supreme Self that has been attained, one should say: "That which is named Space, which is distinct from name and form, bodiless, characterized by being neither gross nor subtle and so forth, and characterized by freedom from evil and the like—untouched by any of the attributes of transmigratory existence, [that] Brahman which is immediate and direct... this is your Self, the innermost of all."
The unseen seer,
the unheard hearer, the unthought thinker.
Unperceived yet perceived, whose essential nature is eternal consciousness, without interior or exterior,
"a mass of consciousness alone," completely full like space.
He possesses infinite power; He is the Self of all,
free from hunger and other such afflictions.

And [Brahman] is devoid of appearance and disappearance; it is the manifester of name and form—which are distinct from its own self, which constitute the seed of the world, which reside within its own self, which are indefinable as being either identical to or different from it, which are perceivable by its own consciousness, and which, due to its inconceivable power, exist merely by their presence in both unmanifest and manifest states. (Samupad II.1.18)
When that name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) was yet unmanifest, it became manifest; from this very Self (*ātman*), the names and forms of space (*ākāśa*) came into being.
And that element called space arose from the Supreme Self in this manner, like foam from clear water.
The foam is neither the water nor is it absolutely different from the water.
Because it is not perceived apart from water,
water itself is distinct from foam, which is of the nature of impurity; likewise,
the Supreme Self is distinct from name and form— which stand in the place of foam— and is pure, serene, and of a different character from them.
When those name-and-form were indeterminate, they became determinate; like foam, they came to possess the designations and shapes of space.
From that state as well, when name-and-form (nāmarūpa) attains a gross condition or undergoes differentiation, it attains the state of air;
from that, the state of fire; and from fire, the state of non-existence.
Then, in this sequence—by the successive entry of each preceding element into each succeeding one—the five great elements arise, ending with earth.
Thereafter, there is earth distinguished by the qualities of the five great elements;
and from that earth, plants such as rice and barley, which consist of the five [elements], are born.
From those two, once consumed, blood and semen connected with the bodies of woman and man are produced.
Both of these, impelled by ignorance and arising from the friction of sexual desire, are infused with mantras and poured into the womb at the time of the menses.
Increasing through the entry of the essence of its own source, it becomes an embryo and is born in the ninth or tenth month. (SamUpad II.1.20)

That [body], once born and having acquired name and form, is consecrated by mantras through the *jātakarma* and other rites; then, through the application of the *upanayana* rite, it comes to be designated as a "religious student" (*brahmacārin*).

That very same body, through the application of the rite of union with a wife, comes to be designated as a "householder" (*gṛhastha*). That very same body, through the rite of forest-dwelling, comes to be designated as an "ascetic" (*tāpasa*).
That very [body], through the conditioning of the cessation of activity, comes to be designated as a "wandering mendicant" (parivrāj);
thus, the body is distinct from you, possessing a different birth, lineage, and conditioning. (SamUpad II.1.21)
The mind and the sense organs are indeed composed of name-and-form (nāmarūpa), according to such scriptural passages as, "For the mind, my dear, consists of food" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.5.4).

And as for how I am devoid of the conditioning factors (*saṃskāra*) belonging to the various classes of birth— listen to this: He who is the animator of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), distinct from the phenomena of name-and-form, he himself,
while animating name-and-form and having created this body, entered here into name-and-form himself, free from the nature of conditioned phenomena, unseen by others.
"Seeing while not seeing, hearing while not hearing, thinking while not thinking, knowing while not knowing—'The Wise One, having fashioned all forms and created names, abides calling them forth.
Regarding this meaning, there are thousands of scriptural passages: "Having created that, He entered into that very thing"; "He has entered within as the Teacher of all people."
“He has entered here,” “This is your Self,” and “He, having split open this very seam, entered through this door.”
“‘This Self is hidden in all beings,’ ‘That deity thought: Come, let me manifest these three deities,’ ‘Bodiless among bodies,’ and so forth. (SamUpad II.1.23)
The Smṛtis also state: "The self alone is all the deities," "The embodied one [dwells] in the city with nine gates," and "Know me also as the Knower of the Field."
“Equal toward all beings,” “the witness and the permitter,” “but the Supreme Person is another,” and so forth.
Therefore, it is established that you are devoid of birth, lineage, and conditioning. // SamUpad_II,1.24 //
If he should say: "I am indeed another—one who is ignorant, happy, miserable, bound, and subject to transmigratory existence; whereas He is another, distinct from me, the non-transmigrating God.
Desiring to cross over the ocean of saṃsāra, I seek to propitiate Him through offerings, oblations, prostrations, and the like, as well as by the duties pertaining to my caste and stage of life."
"How can it be that I am that very same person? // SamUpad_II,1.25 //
The teacher should say: "My dear, you ought not to understand it in this way, because the apprehension of difference has been forbidden.
How has the apprehension of difference been forbidden? To this he says: 'He who thinks, "That one is one and I am another," does not know.'"
“Brahman deserts him who knows Brahman as other than the Self; he goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were multiplicity,” and so forth. (SamUpad II.1.26)
These very same scriptural passages demonstrate that the attainment of the sense of difference leads to wandering in saṃsāra.
And they demonstrate liberation through the realization of non-difference in thousands of places—having established the state of being the Supreme Self in the passage, "That is the Self;
That thou art," and having stated, "The person who has a teacher knows," they show liberation with the words, "For him, there is delay only so long.

Thus, by means of the illustration of the absence of burning and so forth for one who is truthful and not a thief, they demonstrate the cessation of saṃsāra solely from the knowledge of non-difference.
They show that one who intends what is unreal goes to saṃsāra because of the perception of difference, just as in the example of the thief being burned and so forth. (SamUpad_II,1.28)

Furthermore, after stating that "one becomes all" through the vision of non-difference expressed in passages such as "here [he becomes] a tiger," the texts demonstrate across all recensions (*pratiśākham*) that one goes to *saṃsāra* by means of the opposite— the vision of difference— through the statement: "But those who know otherwise than this, having other rulers,
belong to perishable worlds."
Therefore, you have spoken falsely when you said: "The son of a Brahmin, born of the lineage of Adon, is a transmigrating being distinct from the Supreme Self. (Samyukta Upaniṣad II.1.29)
Therefore, because the perception of difference has been prohibited,
and because the undertaking of ritual action has difference as its object,

and because the sacred thread and other such items are means for ritual action— thus making the undertaking of the means for ritual action subject to prohibition— it should be understood that this prohibition is effected through the realization of non-difference from the Supreme Self.
This is because ritual actions and their instruments, such as the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and so forth, are incompatible with the realization of non-difference from the Supreme Self.
For rituals and their instruments, such as the sacred thread, are prescribed for the transmigrating soul (*saṃsārī*),
not for one who perceives non-difference from the Supreme Self.
And its distinctness from that [Self] arises merely through the perception of difference. (SamUpad II.1.30)

Furthermore, if ritual actions were to be performed and not abandoned, [the scripture] would not have taught the realization of the non-difference of the Supreme Self from one's own self— [a Self] which is unrelated to the means of action and unrelated to caste, stage of life, and so forth, which arise as causes for ritual action— by means of definitive statements such as "That is the Self; That thou art."
