Furthermore, he would not have uttered a censure of the realization of difference by saying, "This is the eternal greatness of the Brāhmaṇa," "He is untouched by merit, untouched by evil," "In this state, the thief is no thief," and so forth. (SamUpad_II,1.31)
He would not have taught the state of being unconnected with action— that is, the state of being unconnected with caste and so forth which are caused by action—

nor would he have intended to cause one to abandon actions and the means of action such as the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), if these were not to be relinquished. Therefore, action along with its instruments must be abandoned by one seeking liberation, because they are in contradiction with the realization of non-difference from the Supreme Self.
And the self as well as the other should be understood according to the characteristics as stated in the Śruti. // SamUpad_II,1.32 //
If he should say: "Venerable sir, when the body is being burned or cut, there is direct perception of sensation; and for me, there is direct perception of suffering caused by hunger and so forth."

Furthermore, the Supreme Self is heard of in all the Śrutis and Smṛtis as "free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst," and thus devoid of all the attributes of transmigratory existence. How then could I—possessing characteristics entirely different from that, endowed with numerous attributes of transmigration—realize the Supreme Self as my own self, and myself, a transmigrating being, as the Supreme Self? It would be like perceiving fire as cold.

"And being a transmigrating being, how could I renounce the rites that are the means for attaining all worldly prosperity and the supreme good, as well as the sacrificial thread and other such implements which are the means for achieving those ends?
(Samupad II.1.33)
One should say to him: "That which you said—that when the body is being burned or cut, a sensation is perceived directly as 'mine'—is false.

Why? Because, just as in the case of a tree being burned or cut, the sensation of burning or cutting is perceived in the body, which is the object of perception for the perceiver; therefore, the sensation has the same locus as the burning and so forth."
For wherever burning or cutting is performed, it is precisely there that people designate the sensation of burning and so forth, not in the perceiver of the burning.
How so?
When asked, "Where is your pain? one designates it as being where the burning occurs, saying, "My pain is in my head," "in my chest," or "in my stomach."
The method of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is as follows:

if feeling (*vedanā*) were to exist in the apprehender, or if the cause of feeling (*vedanā-nimitta*), such as burning or cutting, were [present], one would have taught it as the basis of feeling (*vedanā-āśraya*), just as one teaches the basis for burning and so forth. (Samyukta Āgama II, 1.34)
Furthermore, it would not be perceived by itself, like the form (rūpa) that has entered the eye.
Therefore, because it is perceived as having the same locus as burning, cutting, and so forth, sensation (vedanā) is indeed an object of action (karmabhūta), just like burning and the rest.
And because it is of the nature of an entity (bhāva), it possesses a locus (sāśraya), like the cooking of rice.
The formative force (*saṃskāra*) has precisely the same basis as feeling (*vedanā*),
because it is perceived at the very same time as memory (*smṛti*).
Hatred (*dveṣa*), having feeling as its object and the cause of that [feeling] as its object, likewise has precisely the same basis as the formative force.

And so it has been said: "Since passion, hatred, and fear—which arise from cognitions similar to the mental impressions of forms—are perceived as residing in the intellect, therefore the Knower is always pure and fearless. (Samyukta-Upaniṣad II.1.35)
Furthermore, what is the basis for the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth? It is said: that wherein desire and the rest arise.
But where do those desires and so forth reside?
According to such scriptural passages as, "Desire, resolve, and doubt," they reside in the intellect (*buddhi*) alone.
Within that very [intellect], there also exist the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of form and the rest.
For the Śruti says: "In what, then, are forms established? In the heart.
And: "The desires that reside in his heart," and "For he has crossed over."

From hundreds of scriptural passages such as "For this is unattached" and "Or rather, this of his is beyond desire," and from [the Gītā passage] "This is said to be unchangeable," [it is established that the Self is immutable].

“Because it is beginningless and devoid of qualities,” and so forth—desire, aversion, and the like are attributes of the field (*kṣetra*) alone, which is the object, and not of the Self (*ātman*). Furthermore, according to the *Smṛtis*, impurity resides only in action and not in the Self;
therefore, due to the absence of any connection with impurities such as the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of form and so on, you are not distinct from the supreme Self.
Since there is no contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge, it is logical to realize that "I am indeed the supreme Self," as in: "He knew himself thus: 'I am Brahman.'"
“It should be viewed as one alone,” “I indeed am below,” “the Self indeed is below.”
“One should see everything as the Self,” “But where for him everything has become the Self alone,” and “All this is that which is this Self.”
“This very [Self] is partless,” “without interior or exterior,” and “indeed unborn, both within and without.”
“This is indeed Brahman,” “He entered through this door,” and “These are the names of consciousness.”
“Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite”;
“From that, indeed”; “Having created that, He entered into it.”
“The one God is hidden in all beings,” “The bodiless dwells within bodies,” “He is neither born nor does He die.”
“The end of dream and the end of waking,” “One should know that as my Self,” and “He who [sees] all beings...”
“That moves and that does not move,” “Vena beholding that,” “That indeed is Agni.”
“I was Manu and I was the Sun”; “He has entered within as the teacher of all people”;
“Being alone, my dear, [was this in the beginning]”.
This is known from such scriptural passages as: "That is the Truth, that is the Self; That thou art. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7) SamUpad_II,1.37 //
And from the Smṛtis: "The city [is] the living beings... of that which dwells in the cave," "The Self alone is the deities," and "In the city with nine gates."
“Equal toward all beings,” “toward one endowed with knowledge and humility,” and “undivided among the divided.”
From such statements as "Vāsudeva is everything," it is established that you are indeed the one Self, the Supreme Brahman, completely free from all the attributes of transmigratory existence.

If he should say: "O Blessed One, if the Self is 'without interior and without exterior,' 'indeed unborn with both exterior and interior,' and 'entirely a mass of consciousness alone'— like a lump of salt, the Self is devoid of all distinctions of form and is of a single essence like space," then...

"What is this that is seen or heard, whether as the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), or the accomplisher (*sādhaka*)—which is well-known in the *Śruti*, the *Smṛti*, and the world, yet remains a subject of disagreement among hundreds of disputants?
The Teacher should reply: "This which is seen or heard is created by ignorance (*avidyā*);
but from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is only the one Self (*ātman*), which appears as many due to the vision of ignorance."
Like the vision of many moons by one suffering from ophthalmia;
or as it is said: "Where there is, as it were, another," and "For where there is duality, as it were, there one sees another."
“He goes from death to death,” and, “Now, where one sees something else, hears something else, or cognizes something else— that is the finite; and what is finite, that is mortal.”
“Modification is a mere verbal handle, a name,” and “[it is] unreal”;
because the censure of the perception of difference— such as “He is one, I am another”— is thus justified, duality is produced by ignorance, whereas [reality is] “one only, without a second.”
“And because of the scriptural injunctions regarding oneness, such as ‘But where for him... and ‘What delusion, what sorrow? (Samyukta Upaniṣad II.1.40).
If this is so, O Blessed One, for what purpose is the distinction between the means and the goal, and so forth, as well as origination and dissolution, taught in the Śruti? // SamUpad_II,1.41 //

To this it is replied: For one possessed of ignorance—who, having assumed a variety of bodies and so forth, conceives of the self as being subject to the union with the desirable and the undesirable, and who, not knowing through the means [of knowledge] the discrimination between the methods for attaining the desirable and avoiding the undesirable, yet desires both the attainment of the desirable and the avoidance of the undesirable—the scripture gradually removes that ignorance regarding those objects; it does not, however, enjoin a distinction between the goal and the means.

For that saṃsāra is indeed undesirable in nature; thus, by demonstrating the logical possibility of oneness regarding its origin, dissolution, and so forth, it uproots ignorance itself—the very root of saṃsāra—which consists in the perception of difference. When ignorance has been uprooted, through Śruti, Smṛti, and reasoning, [it is established that] "without interior or exterior," "for he is unborn, with both interior and exterior," and like a mass of salt, "he is a mass of pure consciousness."
In this very state—that the Self is of a single flavor and all-pervading like space—the singular wisdom of one who perceives the ultimate reality becomes established;
there, not even a trace of impurity can arise through distinctions such as the production and dissolution of means and ends.

And one who desires to realize this vision of the ultimate truth must renounce the desire for sons, wealth, and worlds—which take the form of the fivefold [set of attachments] produced by the conceit of caste, stage of life (*varṇāśrama*), and so forth.
This is because such conceit is contradicted by correct cognition; furthermore, the logical justification for the prohibition against the perception of duality becomes established.
For once the cognition of the non-transmigratory nature of the single Self has been produced by the scriptures and reasoning, a contrary cognition cannot arise.
For indeed, there is no perception of coldness in fire, nor any perception of old age or death in the body.

Therefore, because all ritual actions and their instruments—such as the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and so forth—are the products of ignorance, they must be renounced by one who is established in the vision of ultimate reality. (SamUpad_II,1.44)
Thus ends the chapter on the procedure for awakening the disciple. // SamUpad_II,1 //

A certain religious student (brahmacārī), weary of the cycle of birth and death and desiring liberation, approached according to the prescribed rite a Brāhmaṇa seated at ease, who was firmly established in Brahman, and asked: "O Blessed One, how shall I be liberated from this cycle of transmigration?
Possessing a body, senses, objects, and sensations, I experience suffering in the waking state; likewise, I experience it in the dream state, only to rest again by repeatedly attaining deep sleep."
Is this my very nature, or is it a contingent state belonging to one who possesses another nature?
If it is my nature, there is no hope for my liberation, because that nature is unavoidable.
Then, for one who perceives omens, liberation would arise from the avoidance of those omens. // SamUpad_II,2.45 //
The Guru said to him: "Listen, my child;
this is not your inherent nature (svabhāva), but is adventitious (naimittika)."
Thus addressed, the disciple said: "What is the cause, what is its remover, and what is my own nature?"
When the cause has been removed, the effect ceases to exist; just as when the cause of a disease is eliminated, the patient returns to his natural state. (Samyukta Āgama II.2.47)
The Guru said: Ignorance is the cause, and knowledge is its remover;
when ignorance has ceased, you will be liberated from the cycle of birth and death characterized by worldly existence, due to the absence of its cause.
"And you shall no longer experience the suffering of dreaming or waking."
The disciple said: "What is that ignorance (avidyā), or what is its object? And what is knowledge (vidyā) which, by removing ignorance, enables one to attain one's true nature?"

The Guru said: "Though you are the Supreme Self, free from transmigratory existence, you have grasped the contrary notion that 'I am a transmigrating being'; though you are a non-doer, you grasp yourself as a doer; and though you are a non-enjoyer, you grasp yourself as an enjoyer."
To regard what exists as non-existent—this is ignorance. (Samyukta Āgama II, 2.50)
The disciple said: "Even though I exist, I am nevertheless not the Supreme Self;
for transmigratory existence, characterized by agency and enjoyership, is my nature, since it is experienced through means of valid cognition such as direct perception."
It is not caused by ignorance (*avidyā*),
because it is impossible for ignorance to have itself as its own object;
for "ignorance" is defined as the superimposition of the attributes of one thing upon another.
Just as one superimposes well-known silver upon a well-known mother-of-pearl shell, or as one superimposes a well-known person upon a post,
or a well-known post upon a person.
The unestablished is not [superimposed] upon the established, nor is the established upon the unestablished;
nor does one superimpose the non-self upon the self.
Because the self is not established;
likewise, [one perceives] the self in what is not-self, precisely because the self is not established. (Samyukta Āgama II.2.51)
The teacher said to him: "No, because of the possibility of deviation.
For indeed, my dear, it cannot be restricted by the rule that one can only superimpose what is well-known upon what is already well-known."

Because we observe the superimposition [of one thing] upon another: for instance, the attributes of the body—such as "I am fair" or "I am dark"—are superimposed upon the Self, which is the object of the notion of "I," and conversely, the object of the notion of "I" is superimposed upon the body in the form of "This I am. (Samyukta Upaniṣad II.2.52)
The disciple said: "In that case, the self is indeed well-known as the object of the notion of 'I', and this body is also well-known.
This being so, there is a mutual superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of the well-known body and the self, just as in the cases of a post and a person, or mother-of-pearl and silver.

Based on what specific distinction, then, has the Blessed One stated that it is impossible to restrict [the relationship] by saying that there is a mutual superimposition of two things already well-known?"
The teacher said: Listen.
It is true that the body and the self are well-known [to all], but they are not as universally recognized as distinct objects of cognition as are a post and a person.
How then?
[This occurs] precisely because [the body and self] are always the objects of non-distinct and non-discriminating cognitions.
For no one perceives the body and the self through two distinct cognitions such that they would think, "This is the body" and "This is the self.
It is for this very reason that the world is utterly deluded regarding the nature of the self and the non-self.
"Whether the self is thus or the self is not thus"—it is with reference to this distinction that I said it is not possible [to know]. (Samyukta Āgama II, 2.54)
Now, is it not observed that whatever is superimposed by ignorance upon something else is unreal in relation to that thing—
just as silver in mother-of-pearl,
or a person in a post?
As in the case of a snake in a rope, or the appearance of dirt on the sky,
so too, through the constant and uninterrupted perception of the body and the self as undifferentiated, there has been a mutual superimposition (adhyāropaṇā) between them.
Therefore, there would necessarily be an absolute non-existence of each of the two in the other;
just as silver and the like, which are superimposed through ignorance upon mother-of-pearl and such, have an absolute and eternal non-existence therein,
and likewise for their opposites in relation to their opposites.
In the same way, the mutual superimposition of the body and the self would be produced by ignorance alone;
this being the case, it would follow that both the body and the self are non-existent,
and that is undesirable.
Because it would fall under the position of the nihilists (vaināśika).
Alternatively, if the body were superimposed upon the self through ignorance (avidyā) by way of the reverse [of that],
then the non-existence of the body would follow even while the self exists.
And that is undesirable,
because it contradicts perception and other means of valid cognition.
Therefore, the body and the self are not superimposed upon one another through ignorance.
How then?
They are eternally conjoined like two bamboo poles. (Samupad II.2.55)
No; for it would follow that [the self] is impermanent and exists for the sake of another.
Because it is a composite, [it is both] for the sake of another and impermanent, just like a bamboo pillar or similar objects.
Furthermore, as for the self imagined by others to be composed with the body, because it is a composite, it exists for the sake of another.
Therefore, the other, which is uncomposite, eternal, and distinct, is established. 2.56.
Since that uncomposite [Self] is superimposed upon the body merely as the body, there arises the consequence of defects such as non-existence and impermanence;
in that case, the defect would follow of falling into the position of the Nihilists (Vaināśikas), namely, that "the body is without a Self."

No; for it is admitted that the self, like space, is inherently uncomposite (*asaṃhata*). Since the self is uncomposite with respect to everything, it would not follow that the body and all other things are devoid of a self.
Just as space, being uncomposite with respect to everything, does not mean that everything is devoid of space, so it is here.
Therefore, there would be no fault of falling into the position of the Nihilists.
Furthermore, as for what was said—
that if the body were non-existent in the self, there would be a contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge—
that is not so.

Because the existence of the body in the self is not perceived through perception and other means of knowledge; for [the body] does not exist in the self, just as a jujube fruit does not exist in a bowl.
Like ghee in milk, oil in sesame seeds, and a painting on a wall.
The body is perceived through perception and other means of knowledge;
therefore, there is no contradiction with perception and the rest.

How then can there be the superimposition of the body upon the self—which is not established by perception and other means of knowledge—and the superimposition of the self upon the body? (Samupad II.2.60)
This is not a fault,
because the self is established by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
For it cannot be restricted that superimposition (*adhyāropaṇā*) occurs only when something is established as occasional, and not when it is established as eternal.
Because we observe the superimposition of surface, impurities, and so forth upon space. (Samupad II.2.61)
"O Blessed One, is this mutual superimposition of the body and the self produced by the aggregate of the body and so forth, or is it produced by the self?"
The Guru said: "Whether it is produced by the aggregate of the body and so forth, or whether it is produced by the Self,
what would that matter to you?"

Thus addressed, the disciple said: "If I am merely the aggregate of the body and so forth, then, because I am insentient, I must exist for the sake of another; thus, the mutual superimposition of the body and the self would not be my own doing.
But if I am the Self, distinct and other than the aggregate,"
"Because it possesses consciousness, it is for its own sake"—thus, by me alone is this superimposition made upon the conscious Self, which is the seed of all misfortune. (SamUpad_II,2.64)
Thus addressed, the Guru said: "If you recognize this false superimposition as the seed of all misfortune, then do not perform it."
"Indeed not, Blessed One; I am unable to act.
Being impelled by someone else, I am not independent. (Samyukta Āgama II, 2.66)
In that case, you do not have your own purpose because you lack consciousness;
rather, that conscious being for whose sake you act and by whom you are impelled, being dependent [on them], is the one who has their own purpose.
"You are indeed Saṃghāṭa."
If I am insentient, how is it that I experience feelings of pleasure and pain, and how do I know what you have said?
The Guru said: "Are you other than that which experiences pleasure and pain as described by me, or are you indeed non-other?"
The disciple said: "I am not, for now, non-different [from Him].
Why?
Because I perceive both of those as objects of action, like a jar and other such things."
If I were not different from them, I would not know both of those;
however, I do know them.

Therefore, it would be something other [than the self]; furthermore, the modification resulting from the experience of pleasure and pain would belong to the self itself, and your own position would be undermined.
If they were non-different,
it would not be logical for those two to have their own respective objects as their referents;
for pleasure and pain caused by sandalwood and thorns do not have sandalwood and thorns as their referents.
Or, the utility of a jar is for the sake of the jar;
therefore, the object produced from sandalwood and so forth belongs to me, the knower of it.
For I am distinct from that [object] and know the entire object as it is mounted upon the intellect. (SamUpad II.2.70)
The teacher said to him: "In that case, you are self-interested because you possess consciousness; you are not impelled by another.

For one who possesses consciousness is not dependent on another and is not impelled by another, since it is logically impossible for one who possesses consciousness to exist for the sake of another who possesses consciousness."
Because of their equality,
like two lights;
nor does the state of being an object for that which possesses consciousness belong to that which lacks consciousness.
Because that which is insentient lacks sentience, it is impossible for it to have a connection with its own purpose;
nor is it observed that two insentient things serve each other’s purposes,
for wood and a wall do not act for one another's sake.
But surely, even though consciousness is common to both, it is observed that the servant and the master stand in a relationship of mutual purpose.
It is not so; for what you intend to express is the possession of consciousness (citimattva) by the Self, just as heat and light belong to fire.
And the illustration has already been shown: "like two lights.
This being the case, you perceive everything as it has ascended into your own intellect, through a nature that is eternally immutable consciousness, comparable to the heat and light of fire.
And if you thus maintain that the self is always without distinction, why have you said:
"Having rested again and again in deep sleep, I experience suffering in the waking and dreaming states"?
"Is this my very nature, or is it merely adventitious?
And: "Has this delusion departed?"
Or what is not? SamUpad_II,2.73.
Thus addressed, the disciple said: "Venerable sir, through your grace my delusion has vanished;
however, I have a doubt regarding my own immutable nature."
How so?
Sound and the other sense objects lack self-established existence because they are insentient.
However, because those cognitions arise with the forms of sound and so forth,
and because it is impossible for those cognitions— which possess mutually exclusive qualifiers such as the forms of blue, yellow, and so on— to be established through themselves,
it is understood that they have external forms as their cause; thus, the possession of the forms of sound and so forth is established by virtue of the external forms.

Likewise, since the various objects that serve as the referents for the "I-notion" (ahaṃpratyaya)—which are themselves composed of causal conditions—are insentient by virtue of being aggregates, it is impossible for them to have their own purpose; therefore, like sound and other objects, their establishment occurs only through being perceived by a grasper distinct from their own nature.

However, because they consist of consciousness when they are not aggregated, the perceptions of the forms of blue, yellow, and so forth, which are the objects of the "I-notions," constitute its own purpose; thus, [the Self] is indeed subject to modification.
There is doubt as to whether it is immutable (kūṭastha). SamUpad_II,2.74.
The Guru said to him: "Your doubt is not appropriate.

Since the very perception of those mental modifications in their entirety and with certainty establishes their unchanging nature and their state as the immutable witness (kūṭastha), you have made the cause of certainty—the perception of all the movements of the mind—the very cause of your doubt."
For if you possessed the quality of transformation (*pariṇāmitva*),
there would be no perception of the mental activity directed toward all its own objects,
just as it is with the mind regarding its own object, or as it is with the sense organs regarding their respective objects.
And yet, for you as the Self, there is no perception of even a single part of your own object;
therefore, you are indeed immutable.

To this, he says: "The meaning of the verbal root [in the word] 'perception' (upalabdhi) is indeed a modification, whereas the state of the perceiver being an immutable self (kūṭasthātmatā)—this is a contradiction. (SamUpad II.2.76)
No; for the term "perception" is used figuratively with respect to the modification that constitutes the meaning of the verbal root.

For that which is the cognition (*pratyaya*) belonging to the intellect (*buddhi*), being a modification consisting of the meaning of the verbal root, culminates in a result that is the appearance of perception of the self; thus, it is figuratively designated by the word "perception.
Just as the act of cutting, culminating in the result of being split in two, is figuratively designated as the meaning of the verbal root.
It is just like that. (Samyukta Āgama II.2.77)
Thus addressed, the disciple said: "But, O Blessed One, the illustration you have given is incapable of establishing my state as the immutable (kūṭastha). How so?"

Just as the act of cutting is conventionally designated as the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) because it culminates in the modification of the object to be cut, so too the mental cognition (bauddhapratyaya)—which is the meaning of the verbal root metaphorically attributed to the term "perception" (upalabdhi)—if it were to culminate in a modification of perception belonging to the Self, would not be capable of establishing the immutability (kūṭasthatā) of the Self.
The Teacher said: "That would indeed be true."
If there were a distinction between the perception and the perceiver,
then the perceiver would indeed be nothing but constant perception itself;
it would not be as in the systems of the logicians, where the perception is one thing and the perceiver is another.
But how can it be that the meaning of the verbal root [in "perception"] culminates in the fruit of apprehension? 2.80.
It is said: Listen!
Was it not heard by you that it was stated [to be] "concluding with the fruit of the semblance of apprehension"?
But I have stated that it does not culminate in the production of a transformation in the Self.
The disciple said: "In that case, how can you say that I, who am immutable, am the perceiver of the mental fluctuations regarding all my own objects?"
The Guru said to him: "I spoke the truth;
by that very [statement], I expressed your state of being the immutable (kūṭastha)."

If this is so, O Blessed One, what fault is mine when, while I— whose nature is that of unchanging, eternal perception— am present, there arise within me mental cognitions in the form of sound and other objects, which terminate in the semblance of the perception of my own nature? (SamUpad II.2.84)
True, there is no fault;
however, I have already stated previously that the fault lies solely in ignorance.
If, O Blessed One,
there is no modification in me as in deep sleep, how then can there be dreaming and waking?
The teacher said to him: "But what is it that you experience constantly?"
"Certainly, I experience it;
however, it is interrupted again and again, not continuous."
The Guru said: "But these two are adventitious; they are not your true nature.
If they were your true nature, like the very essence of consciousness, they would be self-established and continuous.
Furthermore, dream and waking are not your true nature."
Because it would be subject to deviation,
like clothing and such;
for it is never observed that whatever is the intrinsic nature (svarūpa) of something can deviate from it.
However, dream and waking states deviate [from it] because they consist of mere consciousness;
if one's true nature were to deviate in deep sleep,
it would necessarily be sublated as being either destroyed or non-existent.
Because adventitious things, which do not possess that nature [of the mind], are seen to have both characteristics:
for example, the destruction of wealth, clothing, and so forth is observed, while the non-existence of things obtained in dreams or through delusion is also observed. (SamUpad II.2.89)
Surely, O Blessed One, it follows that even the nature of consciousness is adventitious,
because it is not perceived in deep sleep, just as it is not perceived in dreams and the waking state.
Or else, I would be of the nature of insentience. (Samyukta Āgama II.2.90)
No; behold, because that is untenable.
If you view the nature of consciousness as adventitious, behold!
Even in a hundred years, we are not able to conceive of this through reasoning.
Even if it were something other than speech,
because it is a composite entity, its being for the sake of another, its multiplicity, and its perishability could not be prevented by any reasoning;
for we have already stated that what does not serve its own purpose cannot be established by itself.

However, since the Self, whose nature is consciousness, is self-established, its independence from anything else cannot be denied by anyone, because it is never non-existent [in relation to itself]. (Samupad II.2.91)
But has not an inconsistency been shown by me when I said, "I do not see anything in deep sleep"?
No, because it is contradictory. How is it contradictory? For one who sees, the statement "I do not see" is a contradiction.
"Indeed, O Blessed One, never at any time have I perceived consciousness or anything else while in deep sleep.
Therefore, you must be seeing [something] while in deep sleep."
Because you negate only the seen, not the seeing;
for I have said that your seeing is consciousness itself—
that very [consciousness] which, while existing, you negate by saying "nothing was seen."
That vision is consciousness itself; therefore,
because it is never absent from anything, its immutably eternal nature is established by its very own nature,
not dependent upon any means of valid cognition.
For a knower who is established by itself has a dependence on means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the determination of another object of knowledge (*prameya*).
But that other, eternal determination which is required for the determination of something else that is of the nature of non-determination,
is indeed eternally immutable and self-luminous by its very nature.
Regarding its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or as a cognizer (*pramātṛ*), there is no dependence upon another means of valid cognition with respect to it,
because that is its very nature.
Just as luminosity or heat in iron, water, and so forth, depends on something else— such as fire or the sun— [but consciousness does not].
Because they do not have that as their intrinsic nature (atatsvabhāvatvāt),
fire, the sun, and so forth do not depend upon it; for they always possess that as their intrinsic nature.
If it is argued that there can be valid cognition only regarding impermanence and not regarding permanence:

No; for no distinction can be established between the eternality and non-eternality of cognition, since when cognition is valid, no distinction is perceived such that "the cognition of the non-eternal is invalid" while "the eternal [cognition] is valid. (SamUpad_II,2.95)

If it is argued that there would be a distinction: in the case of what is eternal, there is an absence of dependence on a knower; whereas in the case of what is non-eternal, comprehension depends upon [the presence of] effort as an intermediary. // SamUpad_II,2.96 //
In that case, the self as the cognizer is indeed established by itself, independent of any means of valid cognition.
If it is argued that even in the case of non-existence there is an absence of dependence because [the self] is eternal, we say no;
for this has already been refuted by the fact that realization itself exists within the self.
If the establishment of the knower depends upon a means of knowledge, whose desire to know could there be?
That very person who has the desire to know is accepted as the knower.
And that desire to know (pramitsā) concerns only the object of knowledge (prameya), not the knower (pramātṛ);
for if it were directed toward the knower, there would follow the consequence of an infinite regress regarding both the knower and that desire.
For that [desire] as well, there would be another cognizer, and for that one too another;
such is the case when desire has the cognizer as its object.
Furthermore, because the self as cognizer is not separated [from itself], its status as an object of cognition (prameyatva) is untenable.
For in the world, what is called an "object of cognition" is established as being mediated by the cognizer's desire, memory, effort, and the arising of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa);
no other way of apprehending an object of cognition is observed.
Nor can the knower be conceived as being separated from himself by anything— not even by any one of the [mental states] such as desire;
furthermore, memory has the object to be remembered as its domain, not the rememberer.
Likewise, desire has as its object only that which is desired, not the object of the desirer;
for even if it were the object of the desirer— as in the case of the desire of one who remembers— an infinite regress like the previous one would remain unavoidable.
If it is argued that, in the absence of the cognition of the object by the knower, the knower himself would remain uncognized; SamUpad_II,2.100 //
No, for the knower consists of the act of knowing, which has the object to be known as its domain;
if it were to have the knower itself as its domain, there would be an infinite regress as before.
Furthermore, the act of knowing is established within the Self as the eternally immutable light of the Self, independent of anything else.
That [the self] is like the heat and light of fire, the sun, and so forth, has already been established previously.
Furthermore, if the light of consciousness—the nature of awareness—were impermanent within the self, it would be impossible for the self to be its own end;
we have already stated that, because it is a composite of effects and instruments, it would be for the sake of another and would possess defects.
How so?
Because the light of consciousness, which is the Self, would be subject to impermanence within itself due to the intervention of memory and other such factors, it would follow that it is composite.
Consequently, that light of consciousness would not exist in the Self prior to its production or after its destruction.
Because it is a composite entity, like the eye and other sense organs,
it would exist for the sake of another;
and when that [pleasure] has arisen, it exists within the self.
The Self does not possess self-interest [in that sense].
For the establishment of what constitutes the interest of the Self and the non-Self depends upon the presence or absence of those [objects].
Therefore, it is established that the Self’s nature as the light of eternal consciousness is indeed independent of anything else. (SamUpad II.2.101)
But if this is so, how can there be the state of being a knower for a knower when the state of being a knower does not exist? (Samupad II.2.102)
It is said: because there is no difference in the nature of valid cognition (*pramā*) whether it is eternal or non-eternal.
For valid cognition is indeed apprehension (*avagati*).
Whether that [apprehension] is non-eternal—preceded by memory, desire, and so forth—or eternally immutable (*kūṭastha-nitya*), [it remains the same].
No distinction in essential nature exists.

Just as in the case of the meaning of verbal roots such as *sthā* (to stand) and so forth—whether their result is preceded by motion or not, whether it is impermanent or eternal—no distinction in form is found; thus, an identical designation is observed: "men stand."
"The mountains stand," and so forth.
Likewise, even though the cognizer is by nature of the form of eternal consciousness, the designation "cognizer" is not contradictory, because of the commonality of the result. // SamUpad_II,2.103 //

Here the disciple says: Since the Self, whose nature is eternal consciousness, is immutable, agency is not possible for it without being joined with the body and the organs, just as carpenters and others [are not agents] without axes and other tools.
Furthermore, for that which is by nature uncomposite, there would result an infinite regress in the appropriation of instruments and effects;

however, since carpenters and the like are always already composite by virtue of their instruments and effects, there would be no infinite regress in the appropriation of tools such as axes. (SamUpad_II,2.104)

In this case, however, since agency is not possible for that which is by nature uncomposite if it does not take up an instrument, an instrument must be taken up; yet even that taking up of an instrument is itself a modification, so if there were agency in that, another instrument would have to be taken up, and for the taking up of that yet another— thus, if the knower possessed independence, an infinite regress (anavasthā) would be unavoidable.
Furthermore, action itself does not cause itself to be performed, because as long as it has not been brought into existence, it lacks its own essential nature.
If it is argued that another [action], having approached the self, causes the action to be performed, this is not so.
For it is impossible for anything other [than the Self] to be self-established, or to be an object of cognition, and so forth;
indeed, no insentient entity other than the Self is ever seen to be established by its own means of knowledge.
Everything, beginning with sound, is established only as being measured by a cognition that culminates in the fruit of comprehension (*avagati*).
If cognition were something other than the Self, then that too would be a non-composite, self-referential Self and not for the sake of another.

Furthermore, we are unable to conceive of the body, the senses, and objects as being for their own sake, because we observe that their establishment depends upon cognitions that terminate in [the realization of] the Self. (SamUpad II.2.105)
Indeed, for the cognition of the body, one does not require any other means of knowledge such as perception and so forth.

"Certainly; this may be so during the waking state. However, in death and deep sleep, the existence of the body itself is established only in dependence upon means of valid cognition such as direct perception, and the same applies to the sense organs."

For external objects such as sound and the rest are indeed transformed into the forms of the body and the senses; thus, their establishment depends solely upon means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) such as perception.
We have stated that "establishment" refers to the fruit of valid cognition, which is comprehension (avagati);
and that comprehension is of the nature of the light of the Self, which is immutable and self-established. (SamUpad II, 2.107)
Here the opponent objects: "It is contradictory that comprehension (*avagati*) is the fruit of the means of knowledge, while the nature of the Self is an immutable, eternal light.
To him who has spoken thus, [the author] replies: "It is not contradictory. How so?"
Although it is immutably eternal, it is perceived at the conclusion of cognitions such as perception and the like,
because it is for their sake; thus,
when the cognition of perception and so forth is non-eternal, it appears to be non-eternal as well.
Therefore, it is metaphorically designated as "the fruit of the means of valid cognition."
If this is so, O Blessed One, then the realization of the immutably eternal is of the very nature of the self-luminous Self, established by itself,
because it is independent of any means of knowledge regarding the Self.
Therefore, everything else that is insentient is for the sake of another because it acts through combination.

And since its being for the sake of another consists precisely in its nature as the cognition of the conditions of pleasure, pain, and delusion, the existence of the non-self is only in that very form and not in any other form;
therefore, it does not exist at all from the perspective of ultimate reality.

For just as in the world the non-existence of things such as a rope-snake or water in a mirage is observed to be apart from the cognition of them as such, so too it is logical that the dualistic state of waking and dreaming has no existence apart from the cognition of it as such.
It is exactly thus, O Blessed One.
Because the light of the Self (ātmajyotis) is never absent during comprehension, it possesses the nature of being immutably eternal;
furthermore, its state of non-duality exists because it does not deviate throughout the diversity of all cognitions,
whereas the various distinctions among cognitions do indeed deviate from that comprehension.
Just as cognitions in a dream— having the form of distinctions such as blue, yellow, and so forth— are said not to exist in the ultimate sense because they deviate from that [underlying] awareness,

so too the distinctions between cognitions of blue, yellow, and so forth in the waking state must be unreal in nature, as they likewise deviate from that very awareness. And since there is no cognizer other than that awareness, it cannot by its own nature be grasped or abandoned by itself.
And because there is no other [cause]. (Samyuktabhidharmahṛdaya II.2.109)
"It is just so.
This is ignorance (avidyā), the cause of which is cyclic existence (saṃsāra) characterized by waking and dreaming. Knowledge (vidyā) is that which brings this ignorance to an end.
Thus you have attained fearlessness;
henceforth you shall no longer experience the suffering of waking or dreaming,
for you are liberated from the sufferings of saṃsāra.
Oṃ. Thus. (SamUpad_II,2.111)
Thus ends the section on realization. // SamUpad_II,2 //
This enumeration is stated for those seeking liberation who are intent on exhausting the merit and demerit already acquired, and who desire not to accumulate new [karma]:

"The defects have ignorance as their cause; they are the causes for the activity of speech, mind, and body; and from such activity, actions with desirable, undesirable, or mixed fruits are accumulated. This is for the sake of their liberation. (SamUpad II, 3.112)

In that regard, because the objects— sound, touch, form, taste, and smell— are apprehended by the ear and the other sense organs, there is an absence of cognition regarding them either in themselves or in others,
just as there is none for clods of earth and the like once they have undergone transformation;
yet, they are known through the doors of the ear and the other senses.
And that by which they are known is, because it is a knower, of a different nature from them;

for those [objects], such as sound and so forth, possess manifold properties due to their mutual association, including birth, growth, transformation, decline, destruction, conjunction, disjunction, manifestation, concealment, modification, the modifier, the field, the seed, and so on,
and they generally possess manifold properties such as pleasure, pain, and the like.
Precisely because it is the knower of that [intellect], the Knower is distinct from all attributes such as sound and the rest.
In that regard, when being afflicted by the perceived objects such as sound and the rest, the wise person should reflect as follows: // SamUpad_II,3.114 //

Sound, however, [is experienced] through the mere generality of resonance (*dhvani*), or through specific qualities such as the musical notes *ṣaḍja* and so forth; through pleasant words such as praise and the like;
and through unpleasant words such as falsehood, loathsomeness, humiliation, and abuse.

Having made Me—the very nature of vision, unattached, changeless, immovable, deathless, fearless, extremely subtle, and beyond the range of the senses—its object, speech is not able to touch Me at all precisely because of My lack of attachment; for this very reason, there is neither loss nor gain caused by words.
Therefore, what can speech—characterized by praise and blame, or pleasure and pain—do to Me?
For one who lacks discrimination, when sound has been taken as the self, a pleasant sound might increase [his happiness] and an unpleasant one might diminish it;
yet because of his lack of discrimination, he thinks, "But for me, who possesses discrimination, these cannot affect even so much as the tip of a hair.

It is exactly the same with touch in its general form and its specific varieties—such as cold, heat, softness, hardness, and so forth—as well as with unpleasant things characterized by fever, abdominal pain, colic, and the like.

Neither by certain things inherently associated with the body nor by external adventitious causes is any modification— characterized by increase or decrease— produced in me, because of my intangibility, just as the sky is not affected by blows from fists and the like.
Likewise, by means of the generality of form and its particularities— whether pleasant or unpleasant, characterized by female sexual organs and so forth—
no loss or gain whatsoever is produced for me, because I am formless. Similarly,

by means of the generality of taste and its particularities— whether pleasant or unpleasant, consisting of sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent flavors— as they are grasped by those of deluded intellect, [no loss or gain is produced].
No loss or gain whatsoever is produced for me, who am devoid of taste; likewise,
by means of the generality of odor and its specific qualities— whether pleasant or unpleasant, characterized as flowers, ointments, and so forth—
no loss or gain whatsoever is produced for me, who am devoid of the nature of odor.
“[That which is] soundless, touchless, formless, imperishable, likewise tasteless, eternal, and odorless,” according to the Śruti. (SamUpad II.3.115)
Furthermore, those very external objects such as sound and the rest, which exist in the form of the body,
and the internal organs in the form of the ears and so forth, along with the two internal instruments and the forms of their respective objects—
because they are mutually interconnected and because they are composite in all activities.
This being so, for me who am wise, there exists no enemy, friend, or neutral person.
In that regard, if someone, through the conceit of false knowledge, should attempt to bestow upon me something pleasant or unpleasant characterized as the fruit of action,
he bestows that which is truly in vain.
Because he is not an object for me— as the Smṛti says, "He is unmanifest, He is inconceivable"— likewise, He is unchangeable even for all five elements,
because they too do not have Him as their object.

"Based on the Smṛti statement, 'This [Self] is neither to be cut nor to be burned,' even that desire to bestow pleasant and unpleasant things upon My devotees and their opposites— merely by observing the configuration of their bodies and senses—
and the resulting acquisition of merit, demerit, and so forth,"
That [suffering] belongs to those very people,
but not to me, who am undecaying, immortal, and fearless;
for "neither what is done nor what is left undone afflicts him."

This is known from such scriptural and traditional texts as: "He does not increase by action, nor does he become less"; "For he is unborn, both within and without"; and "Being external, he is not tainted by the suffering of the world."
And because a non-self entity does not exist— this is the ultimate reason. Furthermore, the objects of the non-duality of the self [are established] because duality does not exist.
All the statements of the Upaniṣads should be examined, indeed, they should be examined in detail. // SamUpad_II,3.116 //
Thus ends the section on enumeration. // Samyukta Āgama II.3 //

Thus ends the *Upadeśasāhasrī*, the essence of all the Vedas and Upaniṣads, the work of the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpāda, the worshipful teacher and wandering ascetic of the supreme order.
